# Philosophy Quotes, Thinkers & Ideas — Verified and Sourced

Every passage in this archive carries its source — thinker, work, and section — and every recorded line names the wording it came from. Where a quotation is commonly misattributed, the archive says so rather than repeating the popular byline.

[Trace a quotation to its source](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) [Browse the archive](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes)

696 sourced English passages by 146 thinkers across 62 traditions — 58 of them checked against the cited edition, 57 with the original wording recorded. From Plato and Confucius to Kwasi Wiredu, Nishida Kitarō, and Frantz Fanon. [How the levels work](https://www.philosophydef.com/about#verification-levels).

Chance

## Try a random quotation

A passage appears before you choose a theme or thinker, so the encounter can begin with the words themselves. Each refresh draws another from the corpus — and every one of them is sourced.

 Refresh for another passage.

Prefer the generator on its own page? [Open the random philosophy generator](https://www.philosophydef.com/random-philosophy-generator)

How to read

## Sourced first. Chance second.

The homepage withholds selection, and the archive refuses to withhold the citation. Every passage arrives with the work it comes from, so the encounter begins with the words and ends somewhere you can check.

Sourced

Each passage names the work, section, and edition it is cited from.

Checked

58 passages are checked against the cited edition; every page states its own level.

Chance

Each refresh draws another sourced passage from the corpus.

Attribution

## Who actually said it?

Paste any quotation into the [quote source finder](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) to see the located record: the work and section, the wording in the original language, the forms that circulate in its place, and the lines most often attributed to the wrong author. Start with the [misattributed quotations](https://www.philosophydef.com/misattributed-quotes) the archive has already worked through, read how it [sources its texts](https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method), or what it [publishes and corrects](https://www.philosophydef.com/editorial-policy).

## Who Said This Quote? Find the Verified Source

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source

Sourcing and attribution

# Who Said This Quote? Find the Verified Source

A quotation that appears on fifty websites has been repeated fifty times, not verified once. This page does the other thing: it names the work, the section, and — where the passage is translated — the original wording, so the sentence can be checked instead of believed.

## Look up a passage

Paste a sentence, or a few distinctive words from it. Matching runs against the passages this archive has taken back to a located source.

Quotation or opening words

Three steps, in order. Each one catches a different kind of error, and the third is the only one that can end in the answer “nobody said this.”

## How to trace a quote's source in 3 steps

### Step 1. Go to the primary text, not to another quotation site

**Aggregators copy from each other, so a phrase can appear on fifty pages and still have no located source behind it. The first move is always to leave the quotation sites and open the work itself.**

A quotation site is a record of circulation, not a record of authorship. When fifty sites carry the same sentence, that tells you the sentence circulates; it does not tell you someone checked it. Most of them copied from one another, and the earliest link in that chain is often a nineteenth-century anthology, a speech, or a film — which is why so many confidently sourced lines turn out to have no page number behind them.

The practical test: if every page you can find gives the author but no work, no chapter, and no translator, you have circulation and not a source. Stop searching for the quotation and start searching for the work. A quote that genuinely comes from a citable text has a locator, and someone somewhere has printed that locator.

For a philosopher, the author's own corpus is the place to look. If the archive search of a philosopher's complete works returns nothing resembling the sentence, the next question is not “where else is this quoted” but “does this author ever say anything like this.” Those are different investigations, and only the second can end in a negative result.

Reading the surrounding passage is not optional diligence — it is usually what settles the matter. Half of the attribution problems in this corpus resolve the moment you look at the sentence before and after the famous one. Descartes does not write “cogito ergo sum” in the Meditations; he writes “Ego sum, ego existo.” Bacon does not stop at “knowledge and power meet in one”; the aphorism explains that this is because an unknown cause loses its effect. In both cases the truncated version and the located version say different things.

One more trap in this step: search engines are much better at finding the popular form than the correct one. Querying a suspected misquotation will return thousands of pages repeating it, because that is what people wrote down. If you want to find out whether a sentence is in a work, search the work, not the sentence.

Where this step goes wrong

-   The sentence appears on many sites but every one of them gives the same missing locator — that is shared copying, not corroboration.
-   A “source” that turns out to be a film, an advertisement, a self-help book, or a motivational poster rather than the author's text.
-   A source given only as a title with no chapter, book, section, or line — checkable in principle, unverified in practice.

### Step 2. Check the wording against the edition, the translator, and the numbering

**Even a correctly attributed line can be the wrong words. Translation choices, edition differences, and the numbering scheme of the edition you are citing all change what “the source” means.**

A quotation in English from a non-English author has at least two sources: the passage in the original language and the English rendering you are reading. Those are not the same document, and neither is the other's deputy. When someone asks who said a line and what the exact wording is, the honest answer names both.

Translation choices are not cosmetic. Marcus Aurelius' Meditations VI.54 says the swarm, not the hive — the Greek is συμμέλει, the colony, and rendering it as “hive” names the structure instead of the members. That one substitution tilts a Stoic claim about natural membership toward a claim about institutions and conformity. In the Analects, 之 is a pronoun referring back to the Way, and nineteenth-century translators rendered it “the truth”; the resulting English sentence, “they who know the truth,” has been quoted as Confucius ever since, complete with Victorian syntax the Chinese does not have.

Editions matter as much as translations. The Pensées of Pascal are numbered differently in the Brunschvicg, Lafuma, and Sellier editions, so a citation that gives only a section number is unusable unless you also name the scheme. A reader checking “§200” in a Lafuma-numbered edition will find a different fragment and conclude the citation is wrong. Naming the edition is part of giving a source, not a refinement of it.

Where the original is a letter, a speech, or an uncollected note rather than a published book, say so and give the date. “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity” has no page in a printed treatise: it is in Simone Weil's letter to Joë Bousquet of 13 April 1942, and the fact that it is a letter to a specific wounded poet is part of what the sentence means. Filling the gap with the title of an assembled collection is a small lie that makes the citation look tidier and the line look less situated than it is.

When you cannot establish an original, the correct output is not a guess — it is a statement of what is established. Several passages in this archive are recorded as traditional attributions or later paraphrases, because that is what the evidence supports. A source field that says “paraphrase of the idea” is more useful to a reader than a confident chapter number nobody can check.

Where this step goes wrong

-   Citing a section number without naming the edition scheme — different schemes relocate the same fragment.
-   Presenting a translation as the author's words when the English is doing substantial interpretive work.
-   Treating the title of a posthumous collection as the source of a line that appears in a letter or an unpublished note.

### Step 3. Test the attribution itself: occasion, style, and earliest appearance

**Before crediting anyone, ask whether this author had the occasion, the vocabulary, and the opportunity to say it. Three cheap tests catch most misattributions.**

The occasion test asks what situation the sentence would have to arise in. “I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it” is the standard example, and it fails on this test in a specific way: the phrasing is a late-Victorian formulation of a liberal principle. It was written by Evelyn Beatrice Hall in her 1906 biography of Voltaire, under the pen name S. G. Tallentyre, as her own summary of his outlook. Voltaire's actual surviving remark on the subject, in a letter of 1770, is blunter, narrower, and much less quotable — which is exactly why the tidy version displaced it.

The style test asks whether the prose sounds like the author and the period. “They who know the truth” carries the syntax of nineteenth-century English translation; it is not something a Warring States text says. “That which does not kill us makes us stronger” moves Nietzsche's first-person singular German — mich, me — into a plural, and the plural generalises a claim he made about himself. Neither alteration is dishonesty in itself, but both change the sentence's scope, and quoting them as the author's wording hides the change.

The earliest-appearance test is the strongest of the three and the most laborious. Find the oldest document you can that contains the sentence. If the trail consistently runs back to an anthology, a compilation, a speech, or a twentieth-century author rather than to the named source, you have found the real origin and the honest citation is the one you found. Doing this properly sometimes means reading a nineteenth-century translation's preface to discover that the translator's own prose has been absorbed into the text.

The three tests interact, and one failing should make you doubt the others. A sentence that fails the occasion test usually also has a suspiciously tidy style and a trail that stops at an anthology. When all three point the same way, the practical conclusion is not that the quotation is worthless but that it should be presented as what it is: a formulation by someone else, or a summary of an idea, rather than the author's words.

Finally, distinguish a misattribution from a paraphrase. “No one errs willingly” really is Socrates' position in the Protagoras, though the five-word form is a compression; “I know that I know nothing” compresses something narrower in the Apology and adds a paradox. Both are paraphrases, and a paraphrase is not a fraud — it is a paraphrase. The error is presenting it as a quotation, which is why a sourcing page's job is to say which of the two a reader is holding.

Where this step goes wrong

-   A quotation whose earliest traceable appearance is a compilation rather than the named author's work.
-   A sentence that has been smoothed into modern idiom — tidy aphorisms usually have tidy, recent authors.
-   A paraphrase presented as a quotation, which invites the reader to treat a summary as literal wording.

Lines that are widely quoted under the wrong name, and what the record actually supports.

## Commonly misattributed quotations

Each entry below is a quotation this archive has worked through against the cited edition. Where the words are real but the byline is not, the actual writer is named. The full register, with the credited thinkers and why each of them attracts misquotes, is on the [misattributed quotes](https://www.philosophydef.com/misattributed-quotes) page.

1.  > I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Voltaire
    
    **What the record shows:** Evelyn Beatrice Hall (as S. G. Tallentyre), 1906
    
    Hall wrote the sentence in her biography The Friends of Voltaire as her own summary of his attitude. Voltaire's surviving remark, in a letter of 1770, is narrower and considerably less quotable.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0395)
    
2.  > I know that I know nothing.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Socrates
    
    **What the record shows:** No ancient source; a later compression
    
    The Apology has a more careful sentence: where Socrates does not know, he also does not believe he knows. The popular version turns a statement about his own position into a paradox about knowledge in general.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0002)
    
3.  > The heart has its reasons, which reason cannot know.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Blaise Pascal
    
    **What the record shows:** Blaise Pascal — but mistranslated
    
    The French says reason does not know them, not that they cannot be known. The usual English makes Pascal a critic of reason rather than a theologian arguing that discursive intellect has not yet reached what the heart grasps.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0059)
    
4.  > Knowledge is power.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Francis Bacon
    
    **What the record shows:** No Bacon text; a later reduction of Novum Organum I.3
    
    Bacon's aphorism is “knowledge and human power meet in one,” and it continues: because an unknown cause loses its effect. The tag drops the causal claim that is the actual content of the aphorism.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0432)
    
5.  > Moderation in all things.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Aristotle
    
    **What the record shows:** No Aristotelian text; an over-extension of Ethics II.6
    
    Aristotle defines virtue as a mean relative to the agent and then adds that not every action admits one — there is no right amount of murder. The popular maxim asserts the opposite of that qualification.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0436)
    
6.  > That which does not kill us makes us stronger.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Friedrich Nietzsche
    
    **What the record shows:** Nietzsche — with the pronoun changed
    
    The German is first-person singular: “Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker.” Moving to “us” converts a claim Nietzsche made about himself into a general law of resilience.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0070)
    
7.  > Tabula rasa — the mind is a blank slate at birth.
    
    **Usually credited to:** John Locke
    
    **What the record shows:** Earlier scholastic and Aristotelian usage; Locke's own image is “white paper”
    
    The Latin tag is not Locke's and appears nowhere in the Essay. Locke's point in the same chapter concerns the origin of ideas, not the absence of innate powers, and “blank slate” conveys a passivity he did not claim.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0186)
    
8.  > What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Marcus Aurelius
    
    **What the record shows:** Marcus Aurelius — the Greek says swarm
    
    Meditations VI.54 has συμμέλει, the colony, and the image is a body the individual cannot survive leaving. Substituting “hive” names the structure and tilts the Stoic claim about natural membership toward one about institutions.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0102)
    

The questions readers arrive with when they are holding a sentence and want to know whether they can use it.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I find out who really said a quote?

Find the primary text rather than another quotation page. Search the author's own corpus for a distinctive phrase, check whether the work is indexed in full text, and look at the sentence before and after the famous one. If the only pages carrying the line give an author and no work, chapter, or translator, you are looking at circulation rather than a source. The hub page above walks through the method in three steps.

### Why do so many quotations appear on hundreds of sites with no source?

Quotation sites copy from one another, and the earliest link in the chain is often an anthology, a speech, or a film rather than the author's text. Each copy makes the sentence look better attested while adding no evidence. The count of pages carrying a quotation tells you how widely it circulates, never whether anyone checked it.

### What does “quote source” mean?

It means the specific place a quotation can be checked: the work, the section or line, the edition, and — for anything translated — the translator. A complete source for a quotation from a non-English author names both the original passage and the English rendering you are reading, because those are two different documents.

### How can I tell a misattribution from a paraphrase?

A paraphrase compresses or restates something the author did say; a misattribution assigns the words to someone who did not write them. “No one errs willingly” compresses Socrates' position in the Protagoras. “I disapprove of what you say…” was written by Evelyn Beatrice Hall in 1906, not by Voltaire. A paraphrase is not a fraud — presenting it as literal wording is the error.

### Why do editions and translators matter for finding a quote's source?

Because they change the words. Pascal's Pensées are numbered differently in the Brunschvicg, Lafuma, and Sellier schemes, so a section number alone is unusable. Buber's “Alles wirkliche Leben ist Begegnung” is printed in English as both “All real living is meeting” and “All actual life is encounter,” so two people citing the same German line can both be right about the source and disagree about the wording.

### How do I cite a quotation that only exists in a letter or a speech?

Name the letter and its date, or the occasion of the speech, instead of substituting the title of a posthumous collection. Simone Weil's sentence about attention comes from a letter to Joë Bousquet dated 13 April 1942, not from Gravity and Grace, which was assembled after her death. The occasion is usually part of the sentence's meaning.

### Do quotation sites ever cite each other as evidence?

Frequently, and it is the main reason bad attributions persist. A citation that leads to another quotation site has verified nothing. Treat any source that resolves to an aggregator, a listicle, or a poster as an unverified lead and go looking for the work itself.

### What is the fastest check on a suspicious attribution?

Ask what situation the sentence would have to arise in, whether the prose sounds like the author and the period, and where the oldest document containing it sits. The Voltaire attribution fails the first test immediately: the formulation is late-Victorian, and the sentence traces back to a 1906 biography.

### Can a quotation be correctly attributed and still be wrong?

Yes — that is the half-quotation problem, and it is more common than outright misattribution. Cutting “Truth happens to an idea” away from “It becomes true, is made true by events” makes James sound like a relativist. Keeping only “to change my desires rather than the order of the world” drops Descartes' first clause about overcoming himself, and reverses the balance of the sentence.

### How does this archive record a quotation it cannot fully source?

It says so. Passages whose wording circulates without a locatable original are filed as traditional attributions or later paraphrases rather than given an invented chapter number. Where a line is known to be someone else's formulation of an author's idea, the archive page names the actual writer — a fuller answer than a confident citation nobody can check.

## Misattributed Philosophy Quotes — Who Really Said Them | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/misattributed-quotes

Attribution

# Misattributed philosophy quotes

The lines below are quoted constantly, and every one of them is attributed to the wrong person — or to a person who said something narrower, in another language, on a different occasion. Each entry names who usually gets the credit, who the evidence actually supports, and where the located record lives in this archive.

8 entries so far. A line enters this register only after its earliest traceable text has been checked against the credited author's works — not because it appears on a listicle, and not because correcting it would be a good story.

## The register

1.  > I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Voltaire
    
    **What the record shows:** Evelyn Beatrice Hall (as S. G. Tallentyre), 1906
    
    Hall wrote the sentence in her biography The Friends of Voltaire as her own summary of his attitude. Voltaire's surviving remark, in a letter of 1770, is narrower and considerably less quotable.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0395)
    
2.  > I know that I know nothing.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Socrates
    
    **What the record shows:** No ancient source; a later compression
    
    The Apology has a more careful sentence: where Socrates does not know, he also does not believe he knows. The popular version turns a statement about his own position into a paradox about knowledge in general.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0002)
    
3.  > The heart has its reasons, which reason cannot know.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Blaise Pascal
    
    **What the record shows:** Blaise Pascal — but mistranslated
    
    The French says reason does not know them, not that they cannot be known. The usual English makes Pascal a critic of reason rather than a theologian arguing that discursive intellect has not yet reached what the heart grasps.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0059)
    
4.  > Knowledge is power.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Francis Bacon
    
    **What the record shows:** No Bacon text; a later reduction of Novum Organum I.3
    
    Bacon's aphorism is “knowledge and human power meet in one,” and it continues: because an unknown cause loses its effect. The tag drops the causal claim that is the actual content of the aphorism.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0432)
    
5.  > Moderation in all things.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Aristotle
    
    **What the record shows:** No Aristotelian text; an over-extension of Ethics II.6
    
    Aristotle defines virtue as a mean relative to the agent and then adds that not every action admits one — there is no right amount of murder. The popular maxim asserts the opposite of that qualification.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0436)
    
6.  > That which does not kill us makes us stronger.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Friedrich Nietzsche
    
    **What the record shows:** Nietzsche — with the pronoun changed
    
    The German is first-person singular: “Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker.” Moving to “us” converts a claim Nietzsche made about himself into a general law of resilience.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0070)
    
7.  > Tabula rasa — the mind is a blank slate at birth.
    
    **Usually credited to:** John Locke
    
    **What the record shows:** Earlier scholastic and Aristotelian usage; Locke's own image is “white paper”
    
    The Latin tag is not Locke's and appears nowhere in the Essay. Locke's point in the same chapter concerns the origin of ideas, not the absence of innate powers, and “blank slate” conveys a passivity he did not claim.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0186)
    
8.  > What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee.
    
    **Usually credited to:** Marcus Aurelius
    
    **What the record shows:** Marcus Aurelius — the Greek says swarm
    
    Meditations VI.54 has συμμέλει, the colony, and the image is a body the individual cannot survive leaving. Substituting “hive” names the structure and tilts the Stoic claim about natural membership toward one about institutions.
    
    [See the full record and citation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0102)
    

Misattribution concentrates on the famous. The names below are the ones the register credits most often, and each links to the pages where their real, located passages live.

## Why each thinker gets misquoted

Every thinker attracts a different kind of error. Socrates wrote nothing, so every “Socrates quote” is a report by someone else. Nietzsche's aphorisms get shortened until they invert. Confucius arrives through Victorian translations that put nineteenth-century syntax in his mouth. The sourcing profiles name the specific hazard for each author, and what a correct citation looks like instead.

What counts as a misattribution, why philosophy attracts them, and how the archive decides.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a misattributed quote?

A sentence credited to someone who never wrote it. “I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it” is the classic case: it appears on Voltaire memorials, but Evelyn Beatrice Hall wrote it in 1906 as her own summary of his attitude. Misattribution is different from a paraphrase, which restates something the person did write.

### Why are philosophers so often misquoted?

Three reasons compound. Philosophical claims get compressed into maxims, and the compression sheds the argument that gave the sentence its meaning (“knowledge is power” drops Bacon's clause about why an unknown cause loses its effect). Famous names attract anonymous lines, because a quote under a famous name travels further. And most philosophy was written in other languages, so every English version is already an interpretation — one more step away from the text, and one more chance for the byline to drift.

### Is a paraphrase the same thing as a misattribution?

No. “No one errs willingly” is a fair compression of Socrates' position in the Protagoras; a paraphrase becomes a problem only when it is presented as literal wording. “I know that I know nothing” sits on the border: it paraphrases a narrower claim in the Apology, and the popular form turns a statement about Socrates' own ignorance into a paradox about knowledge in general.

### How does this archive decide that a line is misattributed?

By going to the earliest traceable text and checking it against the credited author's own works. Where the line is real but the byline is not — the Voltaire sentence, the “hive” version of Marcus Aurelius — the page names who actually wrote it and what the credited author did say. Every register entry above links to the full record.

### Can I still use a misattributed quote?

You can use it accurately. Either quote the located text with its real source and locator, or present the popular line as what it is — a later formulation, and often a revealing one. The error is not liking the sentence; it is attaching a name to it that the evidence does not support.

Keep going

## Famous Philosophy Quotes | Socrates, Stoics & Confucius

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/famous

Curated selection

# Famous philosophy quotes

A gallery of widely recognized passages — lines that have been read, taught, and argued with for centuries. Each one links to a full archive entry that names the work, the passage, and the edition it comes from.

Famous and well-sourced are different properties. A line can be famous because it circulates, and a famous line can be a compression of something the philosopher actually wrote. The archive entries behind these passages record both: where the words sit, and what forms circulate in their place.

## What makes a philosophy quote famous

Not brevity, and not comfort. The passages on this page survived because they carry an argument in a form that sticks: Socrates refusing exile rather than stop examining lives, Marcus Aurelius telling himself to get out of bed, Descartes locating his own existence inside the one doubt he could not shake. Fame in philosophy is usually the fame of a position a reader can still take sides on.

It also makes them the most misquoted sentences in the language. “I know that I know nothing” is a later compression of a more careful claim; “knowledge is power” drops the clause that made Bacon's aphorism an argument. If you plan to quote one of these lines in print, the archive entry — not this gallery — is the thing to cite, because only the entry carries the locator and the attribution notes.

Suspect a famous line's attribution? [Trace it to its source](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) or check the [misattributed register](https://www.philosophydef.com/misattributed-quotes).

# Short philosophy quotes

Brief English renderings selected for clarity. Useful for teaching, journaling, or a first encounter with a thinker.

Every line below is one sentence or less, and every one links to its located source — the work and passage the wording was checked against, where the archive holds one.

## Short lines, long checkability

Brevity is the test this collection applies, and nothing else. The neighbouring collections answer different questions: [famous](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/famous) is about historical recognition and [best](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/best) is the editors' argument-centred picks. Here the only gate is that the passage fits in a breath and still says something worth thinking about.

A caution worth stating on a page of short quotes: compression is where misquotation begins. Some of the most famous “quotes” in philosophy are short forms that dropped a clause the original argument needed — which is why each entry behind these lines records the wording, the work, and the variants that circulate in its place. If a line is going into print, cite the entry, not the snippet.

## Best Philosophy Quotes | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/best

Editorial selection

# Best philosophy quotes

Not a ranking by popularity alone. These passages were chosen for clarity, argumentative bite, and lasting use in teaching and reflection.

This is the archive's editorial judgement, exercised out in the open. The neighbouring collections answer different questions: [famous](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/famous) is about historical recognition, [short](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/short) is about length. This page is about which passages are worth a reader's first hour.

## How these passages were chosen

Three tests, applied in order. **Argument:** the passage carries a claim a reader could accept, reject, or refine — not a mood looking for a caption. **Clarity:** the English renders the thought without hiding it, and where a translation choice does interpretive work, the archive entry says so. **Use:** the passage repays rereading — it is the kind of sentence a seminar, an essay, or a careful person can build on.

Selection is from the sourced corpus, never beside it: every passage below keeps its work, locator, and edition on its own page, and the popular forms that differ from the text are recorded there too.

## Philosophical Quotes About Love | Plato, Mencius & Modern

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/about/love

Quotes about feeling

# Philosophical Quotes About Love

Philosophers treat love as more than a private feeling: it can be desire, mutual goodwill, recognition, or a disciplined commitment to another’s good. These passages gather that vocabulary without reducing love to a greeting-card slogan.

[Quotes](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes) / [About](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/about) / Love

[What philosophers say about love](#hub-essay-title)

Use these distinctions to compare the passages instead of reading them as interchangeable sayings.

## Love is not one thing in philosophy

Plato distinguishes forms of desire and ascent toward beauty; Aristotle treats friendship as a shared activity of character; later thinkers ask whether love is care, recognition, freedom, or responsibility. Reading the passages together prevents one romantic definition from standing in for the whole tradition.

## How to read these love quotations

Notice whether each thinker describes an emotion, a relationship, or an ethical practice. Then follow the source link: a sentence about friendship in an ethical treatise does different work from a line about eros in a dialogue or a claim about care in modern moral philosophy.

    Symposium 206a

    Nicomachean Ethics IX.4

    Principal Doctrines XXVII

## What philosophers say about love

Philosophy Defined · Last reviewed 2026-09-27

### Eros and the ladder of love: Plato

Plato’s Symposium is the founding text. In it Socrates reports the teaching of Diotima: love (erōs) is desire, and what we desire is “the perpetual possession of the good” (206a). Love begins with one beautiful body and, rightly led, climbs to beauty in all bodies, in souls, in laws and knowledge, and finally to Beauty itself, which “always is, and neither comes to be nor perishes” (210a–212a). The ascent is often read as leaving the individual beloved behind, which is the objection most later theories of love start from.

-   [Plato: love as desire for the good — Symposium 206a](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0006)
-   [Beauty itself — Symposium 211a](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0222)

### Friendship as love: Aristotle

Aristotle discusses love under philia, friendship, in Books VIII and IX of the Nicomachean Ethics. He distinguishes friendships of utility, of pleasure, and of character. The first two last only as long as the use or pleasure does; the third, between people “good and alike in virtue,” is complete friendship, in which each wishes the other well for the other’s own sake. A friend, he says, is “another self.”

-   [Aristotle on perfect friendship — Ethics VIII.3](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0499)
-   [Aristotle: “A friend is another self”](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0014)

### Ordered love: Augustine and the medieval tradition

For Augustine the question is not whether we love but what, and in what order. “Two loves have made two cities” (City of God XIV.28): love of self to the contempt of God, and love of God to the contempt of self. “Love, and do what you will” comes from his homilies on the First Letter of John (7.8), where it means that an act rooted in love for the other’s good may take forms, including correction, that look harsh. Dante ends the Divine Comedy with “the Love that moves the sun and the other stars.”

-   [Augustine: “Two loves have made two cities”](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0234)
-   [Augustine: “Late have I loved you” — Confessions X.27](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0045)

### Graded love or impartial care: the Confucian–Mohist debate

Early Chinese philosophy argued about love’s scope. Confucians held that humaneness (ren) begins at home and extends outward by degrees: “Treat the elders of your own family with reverence, and extend that to the elders of others” (Mencius, Liang Hui Wang I). Mozi answered that partiality causes disorder, and that we should “care for one another impartially” (jian ai). Mencius replied that impartial care amounts to denying one’s own father — the first sustained philosophical debate about whether love should be equal.

-   [Mencius on extending love from one’s own family](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0456)
-   [Mozi: “Care for one another impartially”](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0167)
-   [Mencius: “Those who love others are loved by others”](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0148)

### Love as attention and activity: modern philosophy

Modern writers tend to describe love as something done rather than felt. Erich Fromm: “Love is an activity, not a passive affect” (The Art of Loving, 1956). Simone Weil made attention the heart of it: “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.” Iris Murdoch defined love as “the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real” (1959), which makes love a moral achievement against the self’s tendency to see others only as they figure in its own concerns.

Gabriel Marcel wrote that “to love a being is to say: thou, thou shalt not die,” and Kierkegaard’s Works of Love (1847) argued that love of the neighbour, because it is commanded, is secured against the changes of feeling that end preferential love.

-   [Fromm: “Love is an activity, not a passive affect”](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0478)
-   [Simone Weil on attention and generosity](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0197)
-   [Iris Murdoch’s definition of love](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0200)
-   [Gabriel Marcel: “Thou shalt not die”](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0686)

## Philosophy Quotes About Loneliness vs Solitude | Verified

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/about/loneliness

Quotes about feeling

# Philosophy Quotes About Loneliness & Solitude

Solitude can be chosen for thought; loneliness names unwanted isolation. These passages distinguish independence from abandonment, and ask what community the examined life still requires.

[Quotes](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes) / [About](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/about) / Loneliness

Use these distinctions to compare the passages instead of reading them as interchangeable sayings.

## Loneliness is not the same as solitude

Solitude can be a chosen condition for reflection, creativity, or spiritual practice. Loneliness is usually experienced as a lack of wanted connection. Philosophers therefore ask not only whether a person is alone, but whether that separation supports agency or erodes belonging.

## What philosophers add to the distinction

Ancient ethics tests whether self-sufficiency can coexist with friendship; existential and modern social thought examine alienation, recognition, and the need to be seen by others. Compare the quotations below by asking whether each passage recommends withdrawal, diagnoses isolation, or describes a more demanding form of community.

About this citation

Citations of the Apology in this archive are locators in Plato's dialogue, in which Socrates speaks. The archive files the passage under Socrates because he is the thinker being quoted, but Plato wrote the work, and the citation therefore names Plato and the page says who is speaking. The English wording is the translator's, so the locator identifies the passage while the quoted sentence belongs to a particular rendering of it.

## Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being.”

Ancient Greek

“ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ.”

The Greek word order is “the unexamined life, not to be lived, for a human being.” Most English versions drop “for a human being,” which is where the claim is limited to a human life and not to life as such.

### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “The unexamined life is not worth living.”
-   “An unexamined life is not worth living.”

## Attribution notes

Socrates wrote nothing. This is Plato's rendering of Socrates' speech in the Apology, and the line falls in the penalty phase after the guilty verdict — Socrates is refusing a sentence of silence, not offering a maxim about self-help. Quoting it as a general exhortation to reflection drops the occasion it was spoken on.

[How to trace any quotation to its source](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source)

## Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Plato, Apology 38a and files it under Socratic School.

[What a locator tells you, and what it does not](https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method#locators) · [How this archive traces a quotation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source)

### About Socrates

Socrates (c. 470/469–399 BCE) was an Athenian citizen who wrote nothing and yet redirected Greek philosophy from cosmology toward ethics and the care of the soul.

## Interpretation

Socrates says this while proposing a penalty after his conviction, so it is not a slogan about self-improvement but a claim about what a human life is for. The Greek verb behind "examined" belongs to the practice of testing a claim by questioning it. Socrates is arguing that a life run on untested opinions is not merely worse than a considered one, but not properly human, because the capacity to give an account of oneself is what distinguishes a person from an animal or a machine. The sentence is severe on purpose: he is about to tell the court he will not stop doing this even if acquitted on that condition.

### Why it matters

The test is uncomfortable because it applies to opinions we hold for social reasons. A useful version: take one conviction you defend often, and ask what evidence would change it. If nothing could, you are not holding a view — you are being held by one.

# “What I do not know, I do not claim to know” — Socrates (Apology 21d)

About this citation

Citations of the Apology in this archive are locators in Plato's dialogue, in which Socrates speaks. The archive files the passage under Socrates because he is the thinker being quoted, but Plato wrote the work, and the citation therefore names Plato and the page says who is speaking. The English wording is the translator's, so the locator identifies the passage while the quoted sentence belongs to a particular rendering of it.

## Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“What I do not know, I do not claim to know.”

Ancient Greek

“ἃ μὴ οἶδα οὐδὲ οἴομαι εἰδέναι.”

Literally “what I do not know, I do not think I know either.” The archive's English rendering compresses this to a claim about claimed knowledge.

### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “I know that I know nothing.”
-   “I know one thing: that I know nothing.”

## Attribution notes

“I know that I know nothing” is a later compression, not a sentence in Plato. The Apology passage is narrower and more careful: Socrates claims only that where he lacks knowledge he also does not believe he has it. The popular version turns a claim about his own position into a paradox about knowledge in general.

[How to trace any quotation to its source](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source)

## Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Plato, Apology 21d (later paraphrase of the idea) and files it under Socratic School.

[What a locator tells you, and what it does not](https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method#locators) · [How this archive traces a quotation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source)

### About Socrates

Socrates (c. 470/469–399 BCE) was an Athenian citizen who wrote nothing and yet redirected Greek philosophy from cosmology toward ethics and the care of the soul.

## Interpretation

The sentence summarises Socrates' position at his trial rather than quoting Plato directly: after consulting politicians, poets, and craftsmen, he concludes that his superiority consists solely in not claiming knowledge he lacks. The claim is methodological, not sceptical. Socrates does not deny that knowledge is possible; he denies that he has it, and treats that denial as the starting point of inquiry. The Oracle's saying that no one is wiser becomes, on his reading, a reason to keep examining.

### Why it matters

The distinction worth keeping is between holding a view and knowing it. Most disagreements would shrink if people stated which of the two they were doing.

# “What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee” — Marcus Aurelius

Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VI.54

Thinker

[Marcus Aurelius](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/marcus-aurelius)

## Source record

Translator not recorded — the archive holds the English text but not the edition it came from.

Verification status

Checked against the cited edition, and the wording in the author's own language recorded beside the English. Last verified 2026-09-14.

About this citation

The modern title is a convention; the Greek means 'to himself'. Section numbering differs between editions, so a book-and-section locator should name the edition it follows.

## Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee.”

Ancient Greek

“τὸ τῇ μέλισσῃ μὴ συμφέρον οὐδὲ τῷ συμμέλει συμφέρει.”

The Greek second noun is συμμέλει, the swarm. The standard English rendering says “hive,” which names the structure rather than the colony.

### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee.”
-   “What is not beneficial to the swarm is not beneficial to the bee.”
-   “What is not good for the swarm is not good for the bee.”

## Attribution notes

Meditations VI.54, where the sentence belongs to Marcus Aurelius' argument that he was made for the whole and cannot act against it. The image is a swarm — a body that the individual bee physically cannot survive leaving — and the popular English substitution of “hive” bends it toward a claim about institutions and conformity, which is the opposite of the Stoic point about natural membership.

[How to cite and check Marcus Aurelius quotations](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source/marcus-aurelius)

## Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Meditations VI.54 and files it under Stoicism.

[What a locator tells you, and what it does not](https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method#locators) · [How this archive traces a quotation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source)

### About Marcus Aurelius

Marcus Aurelius (121–180 CE) was Roman emperor from 161 and a practicing Stoic who wrote private Greek notes later titled Meditations. He spent much of his reign on military campaigns along the Danube amid plague and political strain.

## Interpretation

Marcus Aurelius is reasoning against a private, self-contained happiness. The image is from Stoic cosmology: a human being is a part of a larger whole, as a bee belongs to a hive, and a part cannot flourish in a way that damages the whole it belongs to. The line appears in his notebooks as a reminder to himself, which is why it is compressed — it is a rule for daily conduct, not a published argument.

### Why it matters

It supplies a practical test for decisions that feel purely personal: if everyone affected made the same choice you are making, would the arrangement still work? The answer often settles questions that self-interest alone leaves open.

## William James: “Truth Happens to an Idea” — Quote Source (Pragmatism)

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0120

[Quotes](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes) / [William James](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/william-james) / Q0120

# “Truth happens to an idea” — William James (Pragmatism)

William James, Pragmatism

Thinker

[William James](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/william-james)

Tradition

Pragmatism

Work

Pragmatism

Theme

[Truth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/truth)

[Another quotation](#featured-quote) [More from this thinker](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/william-james) [How to verify this source](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source)

## Source record

Work

Pragmatism

Passage

Composed

Not established for this work in the registry

Originally written in

English

English wording

Translator not recorded — the archive holds the English text but not the edition it came from.

Verification status

Checked against the cited edition, and the wording in the author's own language recorded beside the English. Last verified 2026-09-14.

## Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true, is made true by events.”

English

“Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true, is made true by events.”

Two sentences, from Lecture VI, “Pragmatism's Conception of Truth,” in Pragmatism (1907). The second sentence is what the first means.

### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Truth happens to an idea.”
-   “Truth is what happens to an idea.”

## Attribution notes

Quoted at the first sentence alone it reads as relativism — as if anything could become true. James' argument is the opposite: an idea is made true by its verification in events, so the second sentence is not an elaboration but the claim itself. Cutting it off is the single most common way this passage is misrepresented, and readers who arrive looking for the source are usually looking because the one-sentence version seemed to say something James would have denied.

[How to trace any quotation to its source](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source)

## Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Pragmatism and files it under Pragmatism.

[What a locator tells you, and what it does not](https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method#locators) · [How this archive traces a quotation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source)

### About William James

William James (1842–1910) was the Harvard psychologist-philosopher who popularized pragmatism and pioneered scientific psychology in America. Brother of novelist Henry James, he trained in medicine and wrote The Principles of Psychology and The Varieties of Religious Experience.

## Interpretation

This is the core of James's theory of truth and the sentence most often quoted out of his argument. He is denying that an idea is true by corresponding to a ready-made reality and proposing instead that truth is something that happens to an idea when acting on it works out. "Made true by events" means verification is a process in time, not a property an idea already has. Critics have argued this conflates truth with usefulness, and James spent later lectures trying to answer that objection.

### Why it matters

The practical version: treat a belief as a hypothesis whose value is shown by where acting on it leads. That stance makes revision cheaper, since being wrong is information rather than a defeat.

## Terms in this passage

phronēsis Ancient Greek · φρόνησις practical wisdom; sound judgement about what to do

[What epistēmē and doxa means, and the reading it is commonly given](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/episteme-and-doxa)

telos Ancient Greek · τέλος end, completion, the point of a thing

[What telos means, and the reading it is commonly given](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/telos)

## Questions readers arrive with

### What is the source of the quotation “Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true,…”?

“Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true,…” comes from Pragmatism, attributed to William James.

### What does William James mean by truth?

Correspondence, coherence, pragmatist, and deflationary theories compete. Ethics and politics ask who gets to define truth in public life. This passage enters that discussion through truth, action.

### Is the wording of this William James quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true, is made true by events.” Forms in circulation that differ: Truth happens to an idea. / Truth is what happens to an idea. The English reads “Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true, is made true by events.”

### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Quoted at the first sentence alone it reads as relativism — as if anything could become true. James' argument is the opposite: an idea is made true by its verification in events, so the second sentence is not an elaboration but the claim itself. Cutting it off is the single most common way this passage is misrepresented, and readers who arrive looking for the source are usually looking because the one-sentence version seemed to say something James would have denied.

## About Philosophy Defined | How the Archive Is Checked

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/about

About

# Philosophy quotations, traced to where they were written

Philosophy Defined records where a quotation comes from — the work, the passage, the original language — and says plainly how much of that has been checked.

696 passages from 146 thinkers and texts, across Greco-Roman, Chinese, Indian, Islamic, Jewish, Japanese, and Africana traditions.

## What the archive is for

Philosophy quotations circulate detached from their sources, and many of the most shared ones were never written by the person they are credited to. This archive exists to answer the question a careful reader asks next: where exactly does this come from, and does the English say what the original says?

## How much has been checked

Every quotation page states which of the four levels below it has reached. The levels are one vocabulary used across the whole archive — the homepage, the editorial policy, and each passage's own status line all read them from the same register — so a page never claims a check it has not performed.

-   **Original text checked — 57 passages.** Checked against the cited edition, and the wording in the author's own language recorded beside the English.
-   **Edition checked — 1 passage.** Checked against the cited edition, with the circulating variants and the attribution note; no original-language text is recorded in the register yet.
-   **Annotated — 152 passages.** A source locator plus commentary written for the passage; the wording has not yet been collated against an edition.
-   **Recorded — 486 passages.** The English wording and the source as the corpus records them; not yet collated, and kept out of search results until the page carries writing of its own.

## How a record is built

Each passage is filed with its thinker, work, locator, school, and themes. Locators use the reference system scholars use for that author — Stephanus numbers for Plato, Bekker numbers for Aristotle, book and passage for the Analects, section numbers for Nietzsche — so a reader can find the passage in any edition. The details are in the [sourcing method](https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method); selection and correction rules are in the [editorial policy](https://www.philosophydef.com/editorial-policy).

## Where to start

If you are holding a quotation and want to know who said it, use [the quote source finder](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source). To read by person, begin with [Socrates](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/socrates) or [Nietzsche](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/friedrich-nietzsche); by subject, with [the self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) or [love](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/about/love); by work, with [the Meditations](https://www.philosophydef.com/works/meditations) or the [index of works](https://www.philosophydef.com/works). For background, the [guides](https://www.philosophydef.com/what-is-philosophy) and the [glossary of terms](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) explain the vocabulary.

## Editor

**kyree**. Maintains Philosophy Defined and the source records in this archive.

## Corrections

Attributions and locators are corrected when they are found to be wrong, and each correction is listed with its date in the [corrections log](https://www.philosophydef.com/editorial-policy#corrections-log). To report an error, write to [kyreemeng@gmail.com](mailto:kyreemeng@gmail.com) with the page address and the edition you are checking against.

## Why “Philosophy Defined”?

The name says what the archive is for. A quotation is only worth reading once you know where it comes from: which book, which passage, which translation, and whether the person credited with it actually said it. So each record here is traced to its source, and the common misattributions are registered rather than repeated. The [source lookup](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) and the [random generator](https://www.philosophydef.com/random-philosophy-generator) are both still here; the generator is simply the front door to the same archive.

## Editorial Policy | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/editorial-policy

Philosophy Defined is a curated archive. Selection, wording, and attribution are editorial judgments accountable to evidence.

Last updated: 30 September 2026. The archive holds 696 passages: 57 with the original wording recorded, 1 edition-checked only, 152 annotated, 486 recorded only.

## Purpose

The archive presents sourced English philosophy quotations for reading, teaching, and reflection. It is not a substitute for primary texts, scholarly editions, or peer-reviewed commentary.

## Coverage

The curated set spans 696 passages drawn from Greco-Roman, Chinese, Indian, Islamic, Jewish, Japanese, and Africana traditions, with expanded representation of women philosophers. Coverage aims at balanced depth rather than an exhaustive canon.

## Selection criteria

Passages are included when they are attributable with reasonable confidence, philosophically substantive, and clear in English. We exclude political slogans without philosophical content, viral misattributions, and opaque jargon that cannot be responsibly rendered.

## Attribution standard

Each entry records thinker, school, source, and theme. Where scholarly debate exists about authorship or wording, we prefer the most widely recognized attribution and note uncertainty in source fields when needed. Famous lines are not kept merely because they are famous if the attribution is known to be false.

## Verification levels

Every quotation page states its level, and the levels mean the same thing everywhere on the site — the homepage, the About page, and each passage's status line read one shared register:

-   **Original text checked.** Checked against the cited edition, and the wording in the author's own language recorded beside the English.
-   **Edition checked.** Checked against the cited edition, with the circulating variants and the attribution note; no original-language text is recorded in the register yet.
-   **Annotated.** A source locator plus commentary written for the passage; the wording has not yet been collated against an edition.
-   **Recorded.** The English wording and the source as the corpus records them; not yet collated, and kept out of search results until the page carries writing of its own.

Recorded pages carry the corpus wording and source but nothing checked, so they say so and are marked noindex until they carry writing of their own. “Verified” without a level attached is not used anywhere on the site.

## English renderings

Primary display language is English. Renderings are checked against reliable published translations and reference works. We do not invent classical-language wording for display. Where multiple reputable English versions exist, we choose clarity for general readers while preserving philosophical sense.

## Corrections

If an attribution, theme label, or wording is wrong, we correct it and retain the entry when the passage remains suitable. Removed entries are those that fail the selection criteria after review. Duplicate entries for the same passage are merged, and the old address redirects to the surviving page. Report an error to [kyreemeng@gmail.com](mailto:kyreemeng@gmail.com).

## Independence

Editorial decisions are not sold. Affiliate or advertising relationships, if introduced later, will be disclosed and will not determine which quotations appear in the archive.

See also our [sourcing method](https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method) and [about](https://www.philosophydef.com/about#verification-levels) page.

## Sourcing Method | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method

Every quotation in the archive should be traceable to a thinker, a tradition, and a documented English rendering.

Method before virality. A memorable sentence without a responsible source does not belong here. The archive currently holds 696 passages, 58 of them checked against the cited edition — the [level of every page](https://www.philosophydef.com/about#verification-levels) is stated on the page itself.

## Scope of the corpus

Sourcing covers Greco-Roman, Chinese, Indian, Islamic, Jewish, Japanese, and Africana traditions, with expanded attention to women philosophers. Each tradition is represented through citable English renderings rather than exhaustive inclusion.

## Reference hierarchy

We prefer critical editions and widely used translations, then standard handbooks and encyclopedias such as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy for biographical and contextual checks, then reputable historical surveys. Social media and unsourced quote aggregators are not accepted as primary evidence.

## Verification steps

For each candidate passage we ask: Who is the attributed author? In which work or tradition does the line appear? Is the English wording attested in a reliable translation? Does the sentence distort the surrounding argument when removed from context?

Passages that fail attribution or distort meaning are rejected. Passages that survive are tagged with school, source, and theme labels for discovery.

## Locators, and what they establish

A locator is the part of a citation that names where inside a work a passage sits — a book and chapter, a marginal section number, a maxim, a verse, a dialogue and Stephanus page. It is the difference between “Nietzsche said it somewhere” and “Nietzsche, _Twilight of the Idols_, Maxims and Arrows §8”.

What a locator establishes is where to look. It does not certify the English sentence: a passage translated by two hands yields two defensible English renderings of one Greek or German original, and the wording most often quoted online is frequently neither. Where this archive holds a locator, a reader can open the named section and judge the rendering against the text. Where it holds none, the passage page says so outright rather than implying a precision the archive does not have.

Treat any quotation offered without a locator — including ones this archive carries — as a prompt to go and find one.

When the wording matters to an argument, cite the edition you actually read rather than a website that repeats it. Where this archive names a translator, that name belongs in the citation; where it does not, a citation that silently supplies one is fabricating a source.

## Theme labels

Themes are editorial access points for readers, not claims that a historical author used the modern English category. Thin or duplicate theme labels are merged into stronger canonical themes so that theme pages remain useful rather than sparse.

## Biographical notes

Thinker pages that include dates, works, and overviews follow mainstream scholarly consensus (for example, Confucius 551–479 BCE; Socrates c. 469–399 BCE). Where historicity is debated—as with Laozi—we state the uncertainty plainly.

## AI and editorial responsibility

Drafting tools may assist organization, but attributions, dates, and philosophical claims are checked against human-curated sources before publication. The archive’s credibility depends on that review.

## Related

Read the [editorial policy](https://www.philosophydef.com/editorial-policy) and [about this archive](https://www.philosophydef.com/about).

## Random Philosophy Quote Generator | Sourced, Not Random Noise

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/random-philosophy-generator

Chance, then citation

# Random Philosophy Quote Generator

One passage, drawn from 696 sourced English quotations. The draw is random; the source is not optional. Every result names the work it came from, so a line that stops you can be taken further than the screen.

Random selection is not decoration. It is the only way to read a corpus without reading your own taste back out of it.

## Why draw at random

Choosing a quotation is a way of confirming what you already think. Pick a theme and you get the passages that suit the mood you arrived in; search a thinker and you get the thinker you already trusted. Random selection removes that step. It hands you a sentence you did not ask for, from a tradition you did not choose, and asks you to do something with it before context softens it.

That is a reading practice, not a novelty. A corpus this wide — 146 thinkers across the Greek, Chinese, Indian, Islamic, Jewish, African, Japanese, and Latin American traditions — is a collection most readers will never browse evenly. Chance does the browsing. Reading one passage a day at random covers ground a thematic index would never surface, and the sequence is honest: the draw has no editorial preference to serve.

## What makes a generated quotation worth keeping

A random aphorism you cannot trace is worth very little. It can be repeated but not examined, because there is nothing behind it to examine — no argument, no occasion, sometimes no author. The value of a quotation arrives with its locator: knowing that “What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee” sits in Marcus Aurelius' Meditations VI.54, in Greek, in a swarm rather than a hive, tells you what kind of claim it is.

So every draw here is a record rather than a string. The passage arrives with its thinker, its work and section, and a link to the page where the sourced wording is written out beside the wording that circulates instead — plus the attribution problems that attach to it where they exist. If you want to know what happens when you check a line rather than trusting it, the [sourcing method](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) is written out in three steps.

## Ways to use the generator

**Daily reading.** One draw a day, then read the passage's page. A year covers far more of the archive than a theme list would, and you will meet schools you had no plan to open.

**Writing prompts.** Take the draw as a claim you have to argue with, not a sentiment to agree with. The passages that resist agreement are the useful ones.

**Finding a phrase you half-remember.** If a draw is close to something you were trying to recall, [paste the fragment into the source finder](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) and it will match against the passages that have been taken back to a located source.

**Teaching and discussion.** Drawing blind keeps a room from settling on the canonical handful of lines. If you need something more targeted, the [famous](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/famous), [short](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/short), and [best](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/best) collections are curated rather than drawn.

Or choose deliberately

What the generator is, and what it is not.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a random philosophy generator?

It draws one passage at random from a fixed corpus rather than from a list you choose. The point is to defeat your own selection bias: you read something you would not have picked, from a thinker you may not have opened, and the sentence has to stand on its own before any context arrives.

### How is this generator different from a quotation list?

Every draw is a sourced passage from this archive, so a line you like can be taken back to the work, book, and section it came from — and where the wording in circulation differs from the cited wording, or the line is commonly misattributed, the record says so. A random draw you cannot check is just an anonymous sentence.

### Are the quotations really random?

They are drawn uniformly at random from the archive's corpus of sourced passages, with the previous draw excluded so you do not see the same line twice in a row. There is no ranking, promotion, or weighting behind the sequence.

### Which thinkers are in the pool?

All 146 thinkers in the archive, across 93 themes and the major schools. The corpus is deliberately wider than the Western canon: Confucius, Laozi, Mencius, and Zhuangzi sit beside Aristotle and Nietzsche, and alongside Kwasi Wiredu, Nishida Kitarō, Frantz Fanon, Al-Ghazali, and Simone Weil.

### Can I use the generated quotations somewhere else?

Yes — every passage page carries APA, MLA, and Chicago citation formats, and each draw links to its own record. Quoting a sourced line with a locator is the whole reason this generator can exist without becoming another anonymous aphorism machine.

## Epistemology: Knowledge, Truth & Justification | Thinkers & Questions

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology

Branch of philosophy

# Epistemology

Epistemology is the theory of knowledge: what it takes to know something, when a belief is justified, what separates knowledge from lucky guessing, and how far doubt can go.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Epistemology

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 143 sourced passages filed under this branch's knowledge, reason, truth, method, understanding, certainty.

Deep dive: [What Is Epistemology?](https://www.philosophydef.com/what-is-epistemology)

The classical analysis took knowledge to be justified true belief, and most of the field's history is the story of that definition under pressure. Gettier cases showed belief can be true and justified and still not be knowledge; sceptics argued that justification never reaches the strength the definition demands; Descartes made the problem personal by doubting everything that could be doubted and keeping only what survived.

Modern epistemology works on three fronts. The structure question: does knowledge rest on foundations, or on mutual support, or on neither? The sceptical question: what, exactly, do the dream, the demon, and the brain-in-a-vat show — and what do they not? And the social question, urgent in an age of mediated information: when is it rational to take someone's word, and what makes a source worth trusting? The archive's whole sourcing method is an applied answer to that last question.

The branch connects everywhere: science needs an account of evidence, ethics needs to know whether moral claims can be known, philosophy of language asks how words can refer at all, and philosophy of AI now asks whether a system's output can be knowledge for anyone at all.

## The branch's defining questions

-   What is the difference between believing something and knowing it?
-   When is a belief justified, and justification by what?
-   Can radical scepticism be answered, or only lived with?
-   When is it rational to rely on testimony and authority?
-   Can we know our own minds better than anything else?

## Ethics: Moral Philosophy, Virtue & the Good | Thinkers & Questions

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics

Branch of philosophy

# Ethics

Ethics asks how one should live: what makes an action right, what makes a life good, what we owe to others, and which of our responses — to pleasure, to duty, to character — should govern.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Ethics

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 115 sourced passages filed under this branch's morality, virtue, ethics, justice, good, character, friendship.

Deep dive: [What Is Ethics?](https://www.philosophydef.com/what-is-ethics)

The field's three great programmes answer the first question differently. Consequentialism holds that outcomes decide: the right act produces the best states of affairs. Deontology holds that some duties bind regardless of outcome — Kant's formulation makes them follow from respect for persons as ends. Virtue ethics, recovering Aristotle, starts from character: the right act is what the practically wise person would do, and the good life is the flourishing (eudaimonia) of a cultivated character.

The programmes disagree less often than their textbooks imply, but they disagree at the cases that matter: whether consequences can justify a lie, whether duty can survive a catastrophe, whether a virtuous person would even face the dilemma in the same terms. Meta-ethics sits underneath asking what moral claims are — discoveries, constructions, expressions of attitude — and whether moral knowledge is possible at all.

Ethics is also where philosophy meets ordinary life most directly, which is why its passages are the most quoted and the most misquoted on this site. A maxim like “moderation in all things” arrives detached from the argument that qualified it; the archive records the argument.

## The branch's defining questions

-   What makes an action right: outcome, duty, or character?
-   Is there one good life for humans, or many?
-   Do moral truths exist, or do we project them?
-   What do we owe to strangers, and why?
-   Can wrongdoing harm the wrongdoer — and how?

## Logic in Philosophy: Valid Reasoning & Its Limits | Thinkers

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic

Branch of philosophy

# Logic

Logic is the study of good reasoning: which forms of argument preserve truth, why others fail, and how the difference can be made explicit enough to check.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Logic

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 84 sourced passages filed under this branch's reason, inquiry, method, critique, judgment.

Deep dive: [What Is Logic?](https://www.philosophydef.com/what-is-logic)

Aristotle's syllogistic was the first system: if the premises are true and the form is valid, the conclusion cannot be false. That achievement set the discipline's ideal — arguments you can check by shape rather than by charity — and it took until Frege and Russell, in the late nineteenth century, to build the quantificational logic that could actually express mathematics. The twentieth century added modal, temporal, and probabilistic logics, each for questions the classical systems could not state.

Philosophy's interest in logic is not only formal. Deduction preserves truth but never extends it; induction extends it but never secures it, which is Hume's problem of induction and still the deepest unpaved road in the field. Between the two sit the informal failings — equivocation, circularity, false dilemma — that argument in practice actually dies of, and that a reader needs to recognise in the wild.

Logic anchors the other branches because it is where their disputes get decided: a metaphysical claim, an ethical argument, or an epistemological proof is only as good as the reasoning that carries it. The archive's passages quote the reasoning, not just the conclusions, wherever the corpus preserves it.

## The branch's defining questions

-   What makes an argument valid, and sound?
-   Can induction be justified without circularity?
-   Where does formal logic end and informal reasoning begin?
-   Which fallacies do good thinkers actually commit?
-   Are there truths logic cannot express?

Thinkers

## Who works in this branch

[Averroes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/averroes) (5) · [René Descartes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/rene-descartes) (4) · [Paulin Hountondji](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/paulin-hountondji) (4) · [David Hume](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/david-hume) (3) · [Aimé Césaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aime-cesaire) (3) · [Lucretius](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/lucretius) (2) · [Anselm of Canterbury](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/anselm-of-canterbury) (2) · [William of Ockham](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/william-of-ockham) (2)

## Metaphysics: What Exists, What Is Real | Key Thinkers & Questions

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics

Branch of philosophy

# Metaphysics

Metaphysics asks what there is and what it is like at the most general level: what exists, what a thing's identity consists in, whether time and change are real, and where the limits of explanation lie.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Metaphysics

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 130 sourced passages filed under this branch's nature, time, being, god, existence, eternity, soul.

Deep dive: [What Is Metaphysics?](https://www.philosophydef.com/what-is-metaphysics)

The name began as an accident of library shelving — the books “after the Physics” (ta meta ta physika) — and hardened into the discipline's deepest question: what must be true of reality for everything else to be true of it. Aristotle treated it as the study of being qua being; Kant argued that a great deal of traditional metaphysics overreaches what human knowledge can settle; the twentieth century split between those who wanted to dissolve the questions and those who wanted better tools for answering them.

Its standing problems are concrete even when the vocabulary is abstract. What makes a person at time t the same person as at time t′? Do past and future exist the way the present does? Is every event determined by prior events — and if so, what is left of choice? Is there a necessary being, or a first cause? Each question has live defenders on more than one side, which is why the passages quoted here are arguments and not slogans.

Metaphysics overlaps every other branch at its edges: ethics needs to know whether persons are the kind of thing that can be wronged; philosophy of mind needs to know what a mental state would have to be; philosophy of religion asks whether the existence of God can be established by argument. The branch pages on this site cross-link accordingly.

## The branch's defining questions

-   What exists, and what kinds of things are there?
-   What makes something the same thing over time?
-   Are time and change real, or ways of perceiving?
-   Is everything determined — and what would free will require?
-   Why is there anything at all?
