## Philosophy of Education: Learning, Teaching & Formation | Quotes

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-education

Branch of philosophy

# Philosophy of education

Philosophy of education asks what education is for: whether it is the transmission of knowledge, the formation of character, the cultivation of reason, or the practice of the examined life — and what each answer demands of teachers and learners.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Philosophy of education

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 66 sourced passages filed under this branch's practice, education, learning, cultivation, self-examination.

Deep dive: [Philosophy of Education](https://www.philosophydef.com/philosophy-of-education) , [How to Study Philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/how-to-study-philosophy)

The founding answers still frame the debate. Plato's Republic made education the turning of a soul toward what is real, not the filling of a vessel. Aristotle treated learning as habituation: we become just by doing just acts. Confucian tradition made self-cultivation a lifelong discipline in which learning, ritual, and reflection are one practice; Rousseau wanted education to follow nature rather than correct it; Dewey made the classroom a laboratory of experience and democracy.

The modern questions sharpen the old ones. Is the aim knowledge, or autonomy, or flourishing — and who decides? What does equality require of schooling if the point is cultivation rather than sorting? Can virtues be taught at all, the question Socrates' generation already argued, or only practised? And what should a person be able to do with what they have learned: argue, judge, work, or live?

This branch is the quietest of the eleven and in some ways the most practical: every teaching decision inside it answers a philosophical question, whether or not the answer is stated. The archive's passages — Socrates on the examined life, Confucius on learning, Dewey on experience, Arendt on thinking — are the arguments that made the practice what it is.

## The branch's defining questions

-   What is education finally for?
-   Can virtue be taught, or only habituated?
-   What does the examined life require of a learner?
-   Is education for the individual, the society, or both?
-   What makes teaching something other than indoctrination?

## Who works in this branch

[Confucius](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/confucius) (6) · [Wang Yangming](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/wang-yangming) (4) · [Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (3) · [Mencius](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/mencius) (3) · [Xunzi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/xunzi) (3) · [The Doctrine of the Mean](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/the-doctrine-of-the-mean) (3) · [Mary Wollstonecraft](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/mary-wollstonecraft) (3) · [John Dewey](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/john-dewey) (2)

## Philosophy of Language: Meaning, Reference & Truth | Thinkers

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-language

Branch of philosophy

# Philosophy of language

Philosophy of language asks how words and sentences come to mean anything: what reference is, where meaning lives, and what language makes possible — or impossible — for thought.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Philosophy of language

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 60 sourced passages filed under this branch's language, truth, meaning, dialogue.

Deep dive: [Philosophy of Language](https://www.philosophydef.com/philosophy-of-language)

The branch's modern history turns on where meaning sits. Frege gave sense and reference as distinct: “the morning star” and “the evening star” pick out one planet by two routes. Russell analysed definite descriptions; Wittgenstein's Tractatus made language a picture of facts, and his later Philosophical Investigations dismantled that picture in favour of meaning as use — language games, not labels. Austin and the ordinary-language philosophers then noticed that saying is doing: promising, warning, naming.

The American strand ran in parallel: Quine argued meaning could not be pinned down sentence by sentence; Davidson made interpretation the foundation; Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1970) replaced descriptive theories of names with causal chains, and in doing so reshaped metaphysics too. Grice showed how much meaning is carried by what a speaker implicates rather than says — the difference between what the sentence means and why anyone said it.

Two consequences reach far beyond the branch. If thought is structured like language, the study of meaning is the study of thinking; and if meaning is use, then translation, testimony, and quotation — the daily traffic of this archive — are philosophical operations, not clerical ones. Which is why the archive records not just the wording but the forms that circulate in its place.

## The branch's defining questions

-   How do words refer to things in the world?
-   Where does meaning live: speaker, sentence, or community?
-   Can language express everything thinkable — and if not, what then?
-   What is the difference between saying and implying?
-   Does language shape thought, or vice versa?

## Who works in this branch

[Ludwig Wittgenstein](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ludwig-wittgenstein) (7) · [Kwasi Wiredu](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/kwasi-wiredu) (5) · [Kwame Anthony Appiah](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/kwame-anthony-appiah) (4) · [Plato](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/plato) (3) · [Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (3) · [Maimonides](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/maimonides) (3) · [Paulin Hountondji](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/paulin-hountondji) (3) · [René Descartes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/rene-descartes) (2)

## Philosophy of Law: Justice, Rights & Legal Obligation | Thinkers

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-law

Branch of philosophy

# Philosophy of law

Philosophy of law asks what law is and what it claims on us: whether its authority comes from morality or from procedure, what a right is, when obedience is owed, and what punishment could justify.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Philosophy of law

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 88 sourced passages filed under this branch's society, responsibility, justice, politics, conscience.

The central dispute is between natural law and legal positivism. Natural-law theorists, from Aquinas to the postwar revival, hold that law's authority depends on moral merit — an unjust law, Augustine's line runs, is no law at all. Positivists — Bentham, Austin, Hart — hold that what the law is and what it ought to be are different questions, and Hart's The Concept of Law (1961) rebuilt the positivist answer around social rules. Fuller and Dworkin pressed back: law claims to guide by its own moral light, and integrity, not pedigree, is what courts actually apply.

Around that core sit the working questions. What grounds a right — and what happens when rights conflict? Why obey the law at all — consent, fairness, gratitude, or none of the above, as the civil-disobedience literature from Plato's Crito to King's Letter makes personal? What could justify punishment — desert, deterrence, rehabilitation — and what must never be done to a person in its name?

The branch meets the rest of philosophy everywhere: political philosophy supplies legitimacy, ethics supplies the value questions, epistemology the standards of evidence in court. The passages here — Crito, Aquinas, Hobbes, Bentham, Mill, Arendt — are the arguments the modern answers still quote.

## The branch's defining questions

-   What makes a rule law — force, procedure, or morality?
-   Is there an obligation to obey unjust laws?
-   What are rights, and where do they come from?
-   What could justify punishing a person?
-   Can discretion and the rule of law coexist?

## Philosophy of Mind: Consciousness & the Mind–Body Problem | Quotes

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind

Branch of philosophy

# Philosophy of mind

Philosophy of mind asks what a mind is and how it relates to the body and the world: whether mental states are physical, what consciousness is, and what would make something — or someone — persist over time.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Philosophy of mind

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 136 sourced passages filed under this branch's self, experience, mind, soul, thinking.

Deep dive: [Philosophy of AI: Consciousness, Ethics & Machine Intelligence](https://www.philosophydef.com/philosophy-of-ai)

The mind–body problem organises everything. Descartes split reality into thinking substance and extended substance and then had to explain how they interact; the following centuries have been a sequence of answers to that failure — dualist and idealist, behaviourist, identity theorist, functionalist, eliminativist. Functionalism, the currently dominant view, defines mental states by what they do rather than what they are made of, which is what made artificial minds thinkable in principle.

Consciousness is where the agreement ends. Nagel's “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” (1974) made subjectivity the test: a creature is conscious if there is something it is like to be it. Chalmers' hard problem (1995) sharpened it: explaining functions seems to leave the feel untouched. Physicalists respond that the feel will be explained, or explained away; the dispute is exactly as alive as it sounds.

Personal identity belongs to the same branch: Locke grounded the person in memory and consciousness, Hume found only a bundle of perceptions, and Parfit argued identity matters less than we assume. And with AI now producing fluent performance, the branch's oldest question — could this be a mind? — has acquired a practical edge; the archive's philosophy-of-AI guide takes that up in detail.

## The branch's defining questions

-   Are minds physical, and if not, what then?
-   Why is there something it is like to be conscious?
-   What makes you the same person across time?
-   Could a machine have a mind — and what would settle it?
-   How do mental states get their content, their aboutness?

## Philosophy of Religion: God, Faith & the Problem of Evil | Quotes

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-religion

Branch of philosophy

# Philosophy of religion

Philosophy of religion examines the claims religions make and the reasons offered for them: whether God's existence can be argued, how faith relates to reason, and what evil shows about the world.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Philosophy of religion

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 59 sourced passages filed under this branch's faith, god, death, soul, eternity.

Three families of argument structure the field. Ontological arguments, from Anselm on, try to move from the concept of a greatest possible being to its existence. Cosmological arguments — Avicenna, al-Ghazali, Aquinas, Leibniz — press the question of why anything exists and argue to a necessary ground. Teleological arguments read order in nature as evidence of design; Darwin redrew that evidence, and the argument now runs over fine-tuning instead.

Against them stands the problem of evil: if God is omnipotent, omniscient, and good, why is there pointless suffering? The logical form the ancients answered; the evidential form — the sheer amount and distribution of apparently gratuitous pain — is the modern battleground, with theodicies and sceptical theisms on one side and Mackie-style arguments on the other.

The branch also asks the questions believers and sceptics often skip: what “God” would have to mean for any of these arguments to work (the classical theists' answer — being itself — is nothing like an invisible person), whether faith is a substitute for evidence or a response to its absence (Aquinas and Kierkegaard give the two classic answers), and whether mystical experience is evidence. The archive's passages include the theologian-philosophers — Augustine, Avicenna, al-Ghazali, Maimonides, Pascal — argued with, not merely quoted.

## The branch's defining questions

-   Can God's existence be established by argument?
-   What does the existence of suffering show?
-   Is faith compatible with — or prior to — reason?
-   What would a soul be, and is there reason to believe in one?
-   Do religious experiences carry evidential weight?

## Philosophy of Science: Evidence, Explanation & Method | Thinkers

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-science

Branch of philosophy

# Philosophy of science

Philosophy of science asks what science is and why it works: what separates science from pseudo-science, how evidence confirms theories, what a good explanation is, and whether science tells us how reality really is.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Philosophy of science

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 94 sourced passages filed under this branch's nature, reason, method, science.

Deep dive: [Philosophy of Science](https://www.philosophydef.com/philosophy-of-science) , [Philosophy vs Science](https://www.philosophydef.com/philosophy-vs-science)

Induction is the founding problem: no finite evidence proves a universal law, so what makes it rational to believe one? Hume diagnosed the gap; Popper proposed falsifiability as the mark of science — theories must forbid something — and Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) answered with paradigms: normal science works inside a framework until anomalies accumulate, and the shift to the next framework is not a clean logical operation. The Popper–Kuhn argument set the field's agenda for decades.

Explanation is the working core. Hempel's covering-law model said to explain is to derive; then came causal accounts, unification accounts, and mechanisms — the debate matters because it decides what a theory owes you beyond prediction. Underneath sits realism: does a successful theory describe the world's furniture, or just save the phenomena? The pessimistic induction — past successful theories turned out false — keeps the anti-realist answer live.

The branch's questions have become everyone's questions: what counts as evidence in medicine, climate, and economics; how model-based sciences warrant claims; and, most recently, what it means when a machine learns a pattern nobody can state. Science's authority is a philosophical achievement, and this branch is where its warrant is examined.

## The branch's defining questions

-   What separates science from pseudo-science?
-   How does evidence confirm a theory it cannot prove?
-   What makes something an explanation rather than a description?
-   Do successful theories describe reality or only predict it?
-   What happens to a science when its paradigm changes?

## Political Philosophy: Justice, Power & the State | Thinkers & Quotes

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy

Branch of philosophy

# Political philosophy

Political philosophy asks what makes power legitimate: why anyone should obey a state, what justice requires of institutions, and how liberty, equality, and order can be reconciled when they collide.

[Branches](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches) / Political philosophy

A branch is a map, not a fence: most real problems cross the boundaries. The archive holds 138 sourced passages filed under this branch's freedom, society, power, politics, community, equality, liberty.

The classic problem is legitimacy. Plato's Republic made justice the order of a city and a soul; Hobbes' Leviathan (1651) began from a state of nature no rational person could endure and derived absolute authority as the price of peace; Locke grounded government in consent and a right of rebellion; Rousseau relocated sovereignty in the general will. Each answer still has descendants — the arguments on this site are those arguments, quoted where they were made.

The modern debate reorganised around distribution and rights. Mill argued liberty except to prevent harm; Marx asked whose property the state protects; Rawls' A Theory of Justice (1971) revived the social contract as a thought experiment behind a veil of ignorance, and Nozick answered with the minimal state. Feminist, Africana, and postcolonial philosophy then pressed the question every contract theory had deferred: consented to by whom, and at whose exclusion?

Political philosophy differs from political argument by holding its own categories open: what a right would have to be, when obedience is owed, whether equality of what — welfare, opportunity, capability — is the fair measure. The passages here show the reasoning, not only the slogans.

## The branch's defining questions

-   What makes a state legitimate — and when is disobedience justified?
-   What does justice demand of institutions: liberty, equality, or both?
-   What may a majority do to a minority?
-   Is property a natural right or a convention?
-   Can power be separated from domination?

## Branches of Philosophy | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/branches-of-philosophy

Map of the field

# Branches of Philosophy

Philosophy is often mapped into core branches—metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, and logic—plus political philosophy and many specialized fields.

On this page

1.  [The four classical cores](#section-1)
2.  [Political and social philosophy](#section-2)
3.  [Specialized branches](#section-3)
4.  [How to use the map](#section-4)
5.  [FAQ](#faq)

## Short answer

A practical map: metaphysics asks what reality is like; epistemology asks what knowledge is; ethics asks how we ought to live; logic studies valid reasoning; political philosophy asks how power and institutions should be arranged.

## The four classical cores

Metaphysics (including ontology) studies being, causation, time, mind, and what kinds of things exist. Epistemology studies knowledge, justification, perception, and testimony. Ethics studies value, right action, and the good life. Logic studies inference—what follows from what.

These cores overlap. Philosophy of science asks metaphysical and epistemic questions together; philosophy of mind joins metaphysics of consciousness to epistemology of self-knowledge.

## Political and social philosophy

Political philosophy examines justice, rights, authority, freedom, and the legitimacy of states. It is sometimes listed beside the four cores because civic life continually forces philosophical choices about coercion and cooperation.

## Specialized branches

Further fields include philosophy of language, mind, religion, art, law, education, history, technology, and artificial intelligence. Comparative philosophy studies these questions across traditions without assuming a single center.

## How to use the map

Beginners can pick one live question—What is knowledge? What is justice?—and notice which branch it primarily belongs to, then follow quotations and guides in this archive as doorways into fuller texts.

## Frequently asked questions

### What are the main branches of philosophy?

Commonly: metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, and logic, often with political philosophy and many specialized areas.

### Is aesthetics a branch of philosophy?

Yes. Philosophy of art and beauty is a major specialization intersecting ethics and metaphysics of value.

### Where should a beginner start?

Start with ethics or a concrete question you already care about, then widen into epistemology and metaphysics as needed.

## Chinese Philosophy | Confucianism, Daoism & the Way

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/chinese-philosophy

Traditions of thought

# Chinese Philosophy

Chinese philosophy includes diverse traditions that examine ethical cultivation, social order, nature, language, governance, and the way of living well.

On this page

1.  [Confucian thought](#section-1)
2.  [Daoist thought](#section-2)
3.  [Debate, diversity, and influence](#section-3)
4.  [FAQ](#faq)

## Short answer

It is not one doctrine. Confucian, Daoist, Mohist, Legalist, and Buddhist thinkers developed distinct views and debated one another across centuries. Their work is best approached as philosophy in its own right, not as a supplement to a European timeline.

## Confucian thought

Confucian traditions emphasize ren (humaneness), li (ritual propriety), learning, and the cultivation of character in relationships. Ethical life is often understood as practiced through family, community, and responsible public roles.

Thinkers such as Confucius and Mencius explored how moral feeling, education, and good government can support human flourishing.

## Daoist thought

Daoist texts associated with Laozi and Zhuangzi explore the Dao, naturalness, transformation, and the limits of fixed distinctions. They often caution against forcing the world into rigid human categories.

Their reflections on action, spontaneity, and language offer a different model of wisdom: responsiveness to changing circumstances rather than control alone.

## Debate, diversity, and influence

Mohist thinkers argued for impartial concern and practical standards, while Legalist approaches emphasized institutions and state power. Buddhist philosophy, transmitted and transformed in China, contributed major reflections on mind, suffering, and emptiness.

Chinese philosophy continues to shape ethical, political, educational, and ecological conversations worldwide. In this archive, Confucius (551–479 BCE), Mencius (c. 372–289 BCE), Laozi (traditional attribution; historicity debated), and Zhuangzi (late 4th century BCE) are entry points into living traditions rather than a closed museum.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is Chinese philosophy?

It is a family of traditions—including Confucian, Daoist, Mohist, Legalist, and Buddhist currents—that examine ethics, governance, nature, language, and cultivation.

### What is “the Way” in Chinese philosophy?

Dao, often translated as the Way, names a pattern of nature, conduct, or cosmic process rather than a single slogan. Confucian and Daoist uses overlap in the word and diverge in emphasis: cultivated human roles versus alignment with what cannot be forced.

### Who are the main Chinese philosophers to start with?

Confucius and Mencius for Confucian ethics; Laozi and Zhuangzi for Daoist thought. Each is represented in this archive with verified English quotations.

### Is Laozi a historical person?

Traditional accounts place Laozi in the sixth century BCE, but many modern scholars treat the figure as legendary and the Daodejing as a layered compilation.

## Confucianism vs Daoism | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/confucianism-vs-daoism

Comparison

# Confucianism vs Daoism

Confucianism and Daoism are often contrasted as social cultivation versus spontaneous alignment with the Dao—but historically they also conversed, criticized, and borrowed.

On this page

1.  [Ethics and self-cultivation](#section-1)
2.  [Politics and language](#section-2)
3.  [Reading them together](#section-3)
4.  [Side by side](#comparison)
5.  [FAQ](#faq)

## Short answer

Confucian teachings emphasize ren, ritual, learning, and responsible roles; Daoist texts associated with Laozi and Zhuangzi emphasize the Dao, wuwei, and critique of rigid naming and forced order.

## Side by side

| Aspect | Confucianism | Daoism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core ideal | Ren (humaneness) expressed through cultivated roles and ritual | Alignment with the Dao; naturalness over convention |
| Self-cultivation | Study, ritual practice, and reflection within relationships | Unlearning rigid distinctions; wuwei, non-forced action |
| Government | Exemplary virtue and ritual order bring good rule | Restraint and softness; rule that does not over-manage |
| Language | Correct naming (zhengming) clarifies roles and duties | Suspicion of fixed names; the Dao named is not the constant Dao |
| Key figures | Confucius, Mencius, Xunzi | Laozi, Zhuangzi |
| Key texts | Analects, Mencius, Xunzi | Daodejing, Zhuangzi |

## Ethics and self-cultivation

Confucians train character through ritual and study within relationships. Daoist writings often warn that forced moralism can deform life, preferring responsiveness and unlearning of rigid distinctions.

## Politics and language

Confucian political thought links exemplary virtue and ritual order to good government. Daoist counsel frequently praises restraint, softness, and ruling that does not over-manage. Both care about language’s power to clarify or distort.

## Reading them together

Chinese intellectual history is not a simple binary. Many readers held Confucian public roles and Daoist or Buddhist private sensibilities. Comparison should preserve each tradition’s internal debates.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the difference between Confucianism and Daoism?

Confucianism stresses cultivated humaneness and ritual life; Daoism stresses alignment with the Dao and caution about coercive order—though both are diverse.

### Can someone follow both?

Historically, many Chinese thinkers combined resources from both; modern readers can also learn from each without forced syncretism.

### Where should I start reading?

Try Analects passages alongside a short Daodejing chapter or Zhuangzi story, using reliable translations.

# Contact the archive

This archive is maintained by a small editorial team. The fastest way to reach us is email; corrections get priority because a wrong attribution spreads faster than its correction.

Corrections are answered first. Questions about method next.

## Report a quotation error

If a passage on this site is misquoted, misattributed, or wrongly located, write to [kyreemeng@gmail.com](mailto:kyreemeng@gmail.com) with three things: the page address, the edition you are checking against, and the passage as that edition prints it. Corrections that name a checkable edition are acted on directly; the [corrections log](https://www.philosophydef.com/editorial-policy#corrections-log) records every change with its date.

## Ask about a source

If you cannot find the source of a quotation that is not in the archive, the [sourcing hub](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) documents the three-step method this archive uses, and the [thinker sourcing profiles](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) record the specific citation hazards of the most-quoted philosophers. Questions the archive's records cannot answer are exactly the ones the method is written for.

## Reuse and licensing

The quotations themselves belong to their authors and translators. The verification records, source notes, and interpretive text written for this archive may be quoted with attribution and a link to the record you used. For anything larger, ask first.

## Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/doctor-of-philosophy

Academic degree

# Doctor of Philosophy (PhD)

Doctor of Philosophy, usually abbreviated PhD, is a research doctorate awarded for making an original and defensible contribution to knowledge.

On this page

1.  [What a PhD involves](#section-1)
2.  [Why it is called Doctor of Philosophy](#section-2)
3.  [Choosing doctoral study](#section-3)

## Short answer

Despite its name, a PhD is not limited to philosophy. Universities award it in fields such as physics, history, biology, computer science, literature, and sociology. The name preserves an older sense of philosophy as the pursuit of systematic knowledge.

## What a PhD involves

Doctoral study generally combines advanced coursework, independent research, guidance from supervisors, and a dissertation. Requirements vary by country and institution, but the central task is to frame a significant question and answer it through rigorous research.

A dissertation is evaluated not only for effort but for its methods, evidence, argument, and contribution to an existing scholarly conversation.

## Why it is called Doctor of Philosophy

Historically, philosophy included broad inquiry into nature, knowledge, and human affairs. As modern disciplines became more specialized, the doctoral title remained in many fields.

The title does not claim that every PhD holder is a professional philosopher. It signals training in independent inquiry and scholarly research.

## Choosing doctoral study

A PhD is best considered as preparation for sustained research rather than simply a credential. Prospective students should investigate the research fit, funding, supervision, program structure, and career outcomes in their field and region.

The right decision depends on the discipline, the research question, and the opportunities available after the degree.

From the archive

## a priori / a posteriori: from what is prior / from what is subsequent — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/a-priori-a-posteriori

Glossary

# a priori / a posteriori

from what is prior / from what is subsequent

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / a priori / a posteriori

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge) · [Certainty](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/certainty) · [Reason](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/reason) · [Experience](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/experience) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Science](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/science) · [Limits](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/limits)

## What the term does

The distinction between knowledge that can be established without recourse to experience and knowledge that depends on it. In Kant the pair becomes central and is separated from the analytic–synthetic distinction: an a priori judgement is one whose necessity and strict universality cannot be derived from experience, and Kant's question in the Critique of Pure Reason is how such judgements are possible at all. That mathematics and the principle of causation seem to be of this kind, yet deliver information about the world, is the problem the whole critical project is built to answer.

## The reading the sources do not support

Equated with 'analytic' (true by meaning) or with 'innate'. Both equations are later and are exactly what Kant is at pains to keep apart: 7 + 5 = 12 is for him a priori and synthetic, and he argues no innate idea is required.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Michel de Montaigne](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/michel-de-montaigne) (1) , [Socrates](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/socrates) (1) , [René Descartes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/rene-descartes) (1) , [Anselm of Canterbury](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/anselm-of-canterbury) (1) , [Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz) (1) , [Francis Bacon](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/francis-bacon) (1) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1) , [Wang Yangming](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/wang-yangming) (1)

## akrasia: acting against one's own better judgement — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/akrasia

Glossary

# akrasia ἀκρασία

acting against one's own better judgement

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / akrasia

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Will](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/will) · [Choice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/choice) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Morality](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/morality) · [Reason](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/reason) · [Character](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/character)

## What the term does

Akrasia is the condition of knowingly doing what one believes one should not. It is a problem for any theory that treats action as following from belief, which is why Socrates denied it was possible and argued that what looks like weakness of will is really a failure of knowledge in the moment. Aristotle, in Nicomachean Ethics VII, rejects the denial and gives a much more careful account: the incontinent person has the knowledge but does not use it, being moved by appetite or by a belief that holds only in the way a drunk person holds a proverb.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as a failure of willpower in the modern sense. The Greek problem is not that a person lacks strength but that they hold two things at once, which is why the debate was about whether the state is even possible rather than about the remedy for it.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Socrates](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/socrates) (1) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1) , [René Descartes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/rene-descartes) (1) , [Mazu Daoyi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/mazu-daoyi) (1) , [Anselm of Canterbury](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/anselm-of-canterbury) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (1) , [Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz) (1) , [Wang Yangming](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/wang-yangming) (1)

## amor fati: love of fate — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/amor-fati

Glossary

# amor fati

love of fate

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / amor fati

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Fate](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/fate) · [Affirmation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/affirmation) · [Freedom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/freedom) · [Life](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/life) · [Growth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/growth) · [Equanimity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/equanimity)

## What the term does

Nietzsche's formula for greatness in Ecce Homo: to want nothing different, neither forward nor backward nor in all eternity, and not merely to bear what is necessary but to love it. It is the affirmative counterpart to the claim that the world has no purpose outside itself, and it connects to his thought experiment of the eternal recurrence, in which one is asked whether one would will the same life again infinitely. Note that Nietzsche's phrase is Latin, in a body of work otherwise written in German — the maxim is deliberately cut off from the German moral vocabulary he is attacking.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as passive acceptance or as Stoic resignation. Nietzsche's point is the opposite of endurance: resignation still measures the world against what it should have been, and amor fati requires dropping that measure. The parallel with Stoic acceptance is frequently drawn and, on this point, wrong.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1) , [Yunmen Wenyan](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/yunmen-wenyan) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (2) , [Augustine of Hippo](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/augustine-of-hippo) (1) , [Søren Kierkegaard](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/soren-kierkegaard) (1) , [Friedrich Nietzsche](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/friedrich-nietzsche) (1) , [Simone de Beauvoir](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/simone-de-beauvoir) (1)

## anātman / anattā: not-self; the absence of a permanent self — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/anatman-anatta

Glossary

# anātman / anattā

not-self; the absence of a permanent self

Sanskrit / Pali · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / anātman / anattā

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) · [Soul](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/soul) · [Existence](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/existence) · [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding)

## What the term does

The Buddhist claim that no permanent, unchanging self can be found among the constituents of a person — body, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness — and that the belief in one is a source of suffering. The arguments are analytic: take any candidate for the self and it will turn out to be impermanent, and so to be a source of suffering if one identifies with it, and so not to be what one is looking for. The claim is not that persons do not exist but that what a person is differs from what the tradition's opponents take a self to be.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as a denial of personal identity, or as a claim that one does not exist. The point is about what kind of thing a person is — a process rather than a substance — and the practical upshot is a looser grip rather than an absence of concern.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Chandogya Upanisad](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/chandogya-upanisad) (1) , [Heraclitus](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/heraclitus) (1) , [Ovid](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ovid) (1) , [René Descartes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/rene-descartes) (1) , [Yunmen Wenyan](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/yunmen-wenyan) (1) , [Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (1) , [Mazu Daoyi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/mazu-daoyi) (1)

## aporia: impasse; the state of being unable to proceed either way — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/aporia

Glossary

# aporia ἀπορία

impasse; the state of being unable to proceed either way

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / aporia

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Inquiry](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/inquiry) · [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge) · [Limits](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/limits) · [Dialogue](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/dialogue) · [Wisdom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/wisdom) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding)

## What the term does

Aporia is the condition a dialogue reaches when every answer offered has been refuted and none remains. For Plato it is not a failure of the inquiry but a stage of it: the removal of the false confidence that prevented the question from being posed properly. In Aristotle the term is used more narrowly for a genuine puzzle that a theory must resolve, and in later philosophy of language the same word names the point at which a problem resists every available formulation.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic) · [Philosophy of language](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-language)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Michel de Montaigne](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/michel-de-montaigne) (1) , [Socrates](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/socrates) (1) , [Heraclitus](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/heraclitus) (1) , [Martin Buber](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/martin-buber) (1) , [Anselm of Canterbury](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/anselm-of-canterbury) (1) , [Francis Bacon](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/francis-bacon) (1) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1) , [Wang Yangming](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/wang-yangming) (1)

## aretē: excellence, the fulfilment of a thing's own standard — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/arete

Glossary

# aretē ἀρετή

excellence, the fulfilment of a thing's own standard

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / aretē

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Virtue](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/virtue) · [Good](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/good) · [Character](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/character) · [Morality](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/morality) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice)

## What the term does

Aretē is the quality by which something does well what it is for — the aretē of a knife is a good edge, the aretē of a horse is running well, and the aretē of a human being is living as a human being should. It is functional rather than moral in the first instance: the question is always 'excellent at what?', and the answer depends on what kind of thing is in question. Plato and Aristotle both work with this structure, which is why Aristotle's ethics begins from the human function rather than from rules.

## The reading the sources do not support

Rendered as 'virtue', and then read as sexual continence or as rule-following. In Homer, aretē belongs to warriors and to speed of foot; in Aristotle it covers courage and generosity but also wit and the capacity to hold a good conversation.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Philosophy of education](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-education)

## ataraxia: undisturbedness; freedom from disturbance — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/ataraxia

Glossary

# ataraxia ἀταραξία

undisturbedness; freedom from disturbance

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / ataraxia

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Equanimity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/equanimity) · [Contentment](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/contentment) · [Desire](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/desire) · [Freedom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/freedom) · [Attention](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/attention)

## What the term does

Ataraxia is the goal of both Pyrrhonian scepticism and Epicureanism, reached by different routes. The Pyrrhonists hold that it follows from suspending judgement: once one stops deciding that things are good or bad in themselves, the agitation those judgements produce subsides of itself. Epicurus holds that it follows from a correct account of nature — that death is nothing to us, that the gods do not intervene, and that desires divide into the natural and the empty — together with the removal of fear.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as tranquillity or as a pleasant mood. Both schools describe ataraxia as a by-product, not a state to be cultivated directly: in Pyrrhonism, trying to be undisturbed is itself a judgement about how things should be, and it reinstates the disturbance.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy)

## ātman: self, breath, the innermost principle of a person — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/atman

Glossary

# ātman आत्मन्

self, breath, the innermost principle of a person

Sanskrit · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / ātman

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) · [Soul](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/soul) · [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Existence](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/existence) · [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind)

## What the term does

In the Upaniṣads, ātman is the self that survives analysis — not the body, not the emotions, not the intellect, but that in virtue of which the other things are one's own. The teaching of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad that the self is identical with brahman, the ground of the world, is the pivot of the Vedānta traditions, and each school then differs on precisely how the identity is to be read. Buddhism denies the concept outright, which makes ātman the axis of the whole Indian debate about personal identity.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'soul', which imports the Greek and Christian notion of an individual substance created once and immortal. ātman in the Advaita reading is not individual at all — individuality belongs to the level the teaching is meant to undercut.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind) · [Philosophy of religion](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-religion)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## brahman: the ground and totality of what is — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/brahman

Glossary

# brahman ब्रह्मन्

the ground and totality of what is

Sanskrit · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / brahman

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Eternity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/eternity) · [Existence](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/existence) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Spirit](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/spirit)

## What the term does

Brahman names the ultimate reality in the Upaniṣads — the source of the world, that from which things arise and into which they return, and the object of the knowledge the texts are meant to transmit. The etymology relates it to growth and expansion. The Advaita reading treats brahman as without distinctions, so that the plurality of things is a matter of appearance at the level of ignorance; Rāmānuja and others insist that the world is real and related to brahman as body to self. How the two are related is the principal division in Vedānta.

## The reading the sources do not support

Rendered as 'God', which brings in creation, will, and personality from the Abrahamic vocabulary. In the Advaita reading brahman is impersonal and does not create so much as appear as the world.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of religion](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-religion)

## cheng: sincerity, truthfulness, the completion of a thing's own nature — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/cheng

Glossary

# cheng 誠

sincerity, truthfulness, the completion of a thing's own nature

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / cheng

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Sincerity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/sincerity) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Truth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/truth) · [Self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) · [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god) · [Cultivation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/cultivation)

## What the term does

In the Zhongyong, cheng is at once a moral quality and a cosmological one: sincerity is the way of Heaven, and making oneself sincere is the human route to it. Zhu Xi glosses it as 'true and without falsehood' plus 'complete', and the two senses are held together — a thing that is cheng is both genuinely what it claims to be and fully realised in its kind. That is why the text can say that the sincere person develops not only themselves but other things, and why cheng functions as the hinge between the text's account of human nature and its account of the cosmos.

## The reading the sources do not support

Rendered as 'sincerity' and understood as honesty in the interpersonal sense. The Confucian concept includes that but is broader: it is the state in which a thing's actuality matches its nature, which applies to non-human things as well.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Chandogya Upanisad](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/chandogya-upanisad) (1) , [Baruch Spinoza](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/baruch-spinoza) (1) , [Heraclitus](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/heraclitus) (1) , [G. ## conatus: striving; the effort to persist in being — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/conatus

Glossary

# conatus

striving; the effort to persist in being

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / conatus

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Desire](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/desire) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) · [Freedom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/freedom) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Will](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/will) · [Existence](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/existence)

## What the term does

In Spinoza, conatus is the actual essence of a thing: each thing, so far as it can, strives to persevere in its being. It is not a psychological tendency added to a thing but what the thing is, and in human beings it appears as desire together with the striving of mind and body in parallel. From it Spinoza derives an entire ethics — good is what aids this striving, evil what hinders it, and the passions are to be understood rather than condemned. Hobbes uses the same term for the small beginnings of motion in the body, which is a different though related use.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as a life-force or as will to survive. Spinoza's conatus is a definitional claim about what an individual is, not an observation about a drive, and it is accompanied by his denial that anything could have a tendency toward self-destruction.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## dao: way, path, course — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/dao

Glossary

# dao 道

way, path, course

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / dao

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Way](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/way) · [Life](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/life) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Order](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/order) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding)

## What the term does

In classical Chinese, dao is first a road and then, by extension, the course proper to something — the way a ruler governs, the way things proceed, the way to live. In the Daodejing it becomes the name for the unnameable source and pattern of the world, and the text opens by disqualifying its own first line: a dao that can be spoken is not the constant dao. In Confucian usage it is usually more concrete and moral — the way of the former kings, the way of Heaven — and the two senses coexist throughout the tradition.

## The reading the sources do not support

Rendered as 'the Tao' with a definite article, which treats it as a named entity or a being. The Daodejing is explicit that whatever it is, it cannot be named, and Zhuangzi adds that where the road is walked it becomes a road, which is a claim about the relation between path and use rather than about a cosmic thing.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of science](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-science)

## de: virtue, power, the efficacy a thing has by being what it is — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/de

Glossary

# de 德

virtue, power, the efficacy a thing has by being what it is

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / de

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Virtue](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/virtue) · [Power](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/power) · [Character](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/character) · [Way](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/way) · [Cultivation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/cultivation) · [Good](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/good)

## What the term does

De is a thing's own power or potency, and in early Chinese thought it is closely tied to the idea that causing others to follow you is achieved through what you are rather than what you command. The Daodejing's phrase xuande, the mysterious de, describes a power that works without claiming credit and therefore lasts; the Confucian texts use the same graph for the virtue acquired through cultivation. The relation to the older sense of a bestowed favour or a charismatic potency is never entirely lost.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as moral virtue in the Aristotelian sense, which imports the idea of an internal standard of excellence. De is closer to efficacy: it is what makes a thing authoritative in its own domain, and the moral dimension is one case of it rather than the whole.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy) · [Philosophy of education](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-education)

## dharma: the order that sustains things; also one's own duty; also a teaching — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/dharma

Glossary

# dharma धर्म

the order that sustains things; also one's own duty; also a teaching

Sanskrit / Pali · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / dharma

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Morality](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/morality) · [Responsibility](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/responsibility) · [Order](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/order) · [Truth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/truth) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Action](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/action)

## What the term does

Dharma carries three senses that connect: the cosmic order that sustains the world, the specific duty that follows from one's position in that order, and — in Buddhism, where the Pali form is dhamma — the teaching and the constituent factors of experience. In the Gītā the second sense does the work: Arjuna's duty follows from his role, and Kṛṣṇa's argument depends on that duty being tied to a station rather than to a consequence. The Buddhist use is not a duty at all but an analysis of what a person is made of.

## The reading the sources do not support

In English, the word slides almost entirely into the third sense, as in 'the dharma' meaning a teaching, or into a vague sense of cosmic justice. Reading the Gītā through either of those makes its central argument about station and obligation hard to see.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Philosophy of language](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-language)

## elenchus: cross-examination; refutation by question and answer — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/elenchus

Glossary

# elenchus ἔλεγχος

cross-examination; refutation by question and answer

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / elenchus

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Inquiry](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/inquiry) · [Dialogue](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/dialogue) · [Wisdom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/wisdom) · [Humility](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/humility) · [Method](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/method) · [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge)

## What the term does

The elenchus is the method of Plato's early dialogues: Socrates asks what a term means, takes the answer offered, and by further questions draws the respondent into contradicting it. The result is not a definition but a demonstration that the respondent did not know what they claimed to know. Whether it is a method for discovering truth or only for exposing false confidence is disputed, and the dialogues themselves leave the question open — most of them end without a positive answer.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as a technique for winning arguments. Its distinguishing feature is that Socrates counts himself among the ignorant and that the outcome is usually aporia rather than victory.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic) · [Philosophy of language](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-language)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## epistēmē and doxa: knowledge and opinion — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/episteme-and-doxa

Glossary

# epistēmē and doxa ἐπιστήμη / δόξα

knowledge and opinion

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / epistēmē and doxa

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge) · [Truth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/truth) · [Certainty](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/certainty) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Experience](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/experience) · [Science](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/science)

## What the term does

The distinction Plato draws in the Republic and the Theaetetus, and the one most of Western epistemology inherits. Doxa is a belief that could be otherwise and can be false; epistēmē is knowledge of what cannot be otherwise, and Plato requires that it be tied down by an account of why it is true. In the Republic the two are correlated with their objects — opinion with the changing sensible world, knowledge with the unchanging intelligible one — which is why Plato's theory of knowledge cannot be separated from his metaphysics. The Theaetetus works through and rejects three definitions of knowledge without settling on a fourth.

## The reading the sources do not support

Doxa is commonly translated 'opinion', which in English suggests a low-confidence personal view. The Greek term covers everything from a guess to a firm and well-grounded belief, and its opposite is the changelessness of the object, not the confidence of the holder.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind) · [Philosophy of language](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-language)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## epochē: suspension of judgement — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/epoche

Glossary

# epochē ἐποχή

suspension of judgement

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / epochē

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Certainty](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/certainty) · [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge) · [Judgment](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/judgment) · [Inquiry](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/inquiry) · [Experience](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/experience) · [Equanimity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/equanimity)

## What the term does

In Pyrrhonian scepticism, epochē is the withholding of assent that follows from the equal strength of opposing arguments — a practical discipline for reaching ataraxia, not a theoretical conclusion about our capacities. Husserl chose the same word for a different operation in phenomenology: the bracketing of the 'natural attitude', in which one sets aside the question of whether the world exists in order to describe how it is given to consciousness.

## The reading the sources do not support

The two senses are routinely conflated, and the difference is not cosmetic. The Pyrrhonian epochē aims at disengagement from belief; Husserl's aims at a more exact description of experience, and it presupposes that something can be described. Quoting one as the other is one of the more common errors in popular writing about both.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Michel de Montaigne](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/michel-de-montaigne) (1) , [Socrates](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/socrates) (1) , [Heraclitus](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/heraclitus) (1) , [René Descartes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/rene-descartes) (1) , [Anselm of Canterbury](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/anselm-of-canterbury) (1) , [Francis Bacon](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/francis-bacon) (1) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1) , [Wang Yangming](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/wang-yangming) (1)

## esse and essentia: existence and essence — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/esse-and-essentia

Glossary

# esse and essentia

existence and essence

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / esse and essentia

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Existence](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/existence) · [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Truth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/truth)

## What the term does

The distinction between that a thing is and what it is, which medieval philosophy inherits from Aristotle's distinction between existence and what-it-is-to-be and turns into a central question. Aquinas argues that in anything other than God essence and existence are really distinct, so that a creature's existence is received rather than included in its nature — which is what makes it possible to say why there is something rather than nothing about any particular thing. In God alone, on this account, essence and existence are identical.

## The reading the sources do not support

Treated as the difference between a thing and its definition, which makes the claim sound like a verbal point. The Thomist claim is metaphysical: nothing about what a finite thing is entails that it exists.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of language](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-language)

## Thinkers who work with this term

Hegel](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/g-w-f-hegel) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (1) , [Nishitani Keiji](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/nishitani-keiji) (1) , [Voltaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/voltaire) (1) , [George Berkeley](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/george-berkeley) (1) , [Giambattista Vico](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/giambattista-vico) (1) , [Ralph Waldo Emerson](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ralph-waldo-emerson) (1)

## eudaimonia: living well and doing well; human flourishing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/eudaimonia

Glossary

# eudaimonia εὐδαιμονία

living well and doing well; human flourishing

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / eudaimonia

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Happiness](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/happiness) · [Good](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/good) · [Life](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/life) · [Virtue](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/virtue) · [Contentment](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/contentment) · [Meaning](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/meaning) · [Living](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/living)

## What the term does

Eudaimonia names the condition of a life going well taken as a whole, not a feeling at a moment. Aristotle treats it as the highest good because it is what everything else is wanted for and it is not wanted for the sake of anything further. It is constituted by activity over a complete life rather than by a state one can be put into, which is why Aristotle says one swallow does not make a spring and cannot call a person happy until the life is over.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'happiness', which in modern English denotes a feeling of satisfaction. That reading makes eudaimonia something one can be given, and makes Aristotle's claim that it takes a whole life to assess it sound absurd. 'Flourishing' is the ordinary scholarly substitute, and it is chosen precisely to drop the feeling.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Philosophy of language](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-language)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## habitus: a settled state; a durable disposition — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/habitus

Glossary

# habitus

a settled state; a durable disposition

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / habitus

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Character](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/character) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Virtue](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/virtue) · [Habit](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/habit) · [Cultivation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/cultivation) · [Action](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/action)

## What the term does

The Latin rendering of Aristotle's hexis: a stable condition of a thing that disposes it to act in a certain way, as distinct from a passing mood or a capacity one merely has. Virtues and vices are habitus, which is why Aristotle says virtue is acquired by doing the corresponding act until the disposition settles. In medieval theology habitus becomes central to the analysis of grace as a quality infused in the soul, and in twentieth-century sociology Bourdieu revives the term for the durable dispositions acquired through one's position in a social field.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as 'habit' in the everyday sense of a repeated behaviour. A habitus is a disposition that explains the behaviour, not the repetition of the behaviour itself, and it can be operative without being noticed by the person who has it.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Philosophy of education](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-education)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (1) , [Xunzi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/xunzi) (1) , [Mazu Daoyi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/mazu-daoyi) (1) , [Voltaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/voltaire) (1) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (1) , [Wang Yangming](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/wang-yangming) (1) , [Horace](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/horace) (1) , [Plato](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/plato) (1)

## ijtihād: exerting oneself to derive a ruling; independent legal reasoning — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/ijtihad

Glossary

# ijtihād اجتهاد

exerting oneself to derive a ruling; independent legal reasoning

Arabic · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / ijtihād

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Reason](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/reason) · [Method](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/method) · [Justice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/justice) · [Inquiry](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/inquiry) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Judgment](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/judgment)

## What the term does

Ijtihād is the effort of a qualified jurist to reach a legal ruling on a question the received texts do not settle directly, by reasoning from the sources. It sits opposite taqlīd, the following of an established ruling. The extent to which ijtihād remains possible — the so-called closing of the gate, and whether it ever closed — is a modern historical question rather than a settled one, and the claim that it closed is itself a claim made at a particular time by particular jurists. The concept matters philosophically because it makes the derivation of law a rational activity with standards, not an act of retrieval.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'interpretation' or as 'reform', and then attached to a single modern movement. Historically it is an ordinary part of the juristic method, and every major school of law depends on it for the cases its founding texts did not cover.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic)

# Glossary of philosophical terms

52 terms that the archive's quotations use in a technical sense, in the language they came from.

49 of the 52 entries carry a specific misreading: a translation that hardened into a false equivalence and now circulates as though it were the text.

The archive's quotations are English renderings of Greek, Chinese, Sanskrit, Arabic, Hebrew, German, and French. Transliteration alone cannot carry that, so each entry names the original alongside the gloss.

## How to use this glossary

Reach for an entry when a quotation uses a word you suspect is doing more work than its English equivalent admits. Each page gives what the term does in the argument it belongs to, what it is commonly mistranslated as, and where in the archive it is in play. The terms are not a dictionary: they are the words a reader of this corpus actually trips over.

## intellectus and ratio: intellective apprehension and discursive reason — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/intellectus-and-ratio

Glossary

# intellectus and ratio

intellective apprehension and discursive reason

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / intellectus and ratio

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Reason](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/reason) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind) · [Thinking](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/thinking) · [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge)

## What the term does

The two modes of rational cognition distinguished in medieval philosophy. Ratio proceeds step by step from premises to conclusion and is what we employ in inference and argument; intellectus grasps a principle or a whole directly, without movement. Aquinas holds that they are distinct operations of the same power and that intellectus is higher, because the discursive thinker is still on the way to something the other already holds. The distinction is the Latin form of Aristotle's nous and dianoia, and it drives the medieval claim that theology can be a science even though its first principles are believed rather than demonstrated.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)
