## junzi: the noble person, literally 'son of a lord' — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/junzi

Glossary

# junzi 君子

the noble person, literally 'son of a lord'

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / junzi

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Character](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/character) · [Virtue](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/virtue) · [Gentleman](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/gentleman) · [Self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) · [Cultivation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/cultivation) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/ethics) · [Good](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/good)

## What the term does

Junzi originally denoted hereditary rank: the son of a ruler. Confucius relocates the term, so that it designates the person of developed moral character whether or not they hold office — a change of reference that is one of the most consequential moves in the Analects, because it makes nobility a matter of cultivation rather than of birth. Most of the text's teaching is addressed to the junzi in this second sense, in contrast with the xiaoren, the small person, whose concern is profit and whose standard is what others will think.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'gentleman', which carries an English class connotation and a tone of mild good manners. The junzi is defined by what they would do under pressure, and the contrast with the xiaoren is a contrast of ethical orientation rather than of social bearing.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind) · [Philosophy of education](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-education)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Chandogya Upanisad](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/chandogya-upanisad) (1) , [Heraclitus](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/heraclitus) (1) , [Ovid](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ovid) (1) , [Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (2) , [René Descartes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/rene-descartes) (1) , [Yunmen Wenyan](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/yunmen-wenyan) (1) , [Xunzi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/xunzi) (1)

## Primary sources in this archive

-   [Nicomachean Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/works/nicomachean-ethics) — Ἠθικὰ Νικομάχεια
-   [Discourse on the Method](https://www.philosophydef.com/works/discourse-on-the-method) — Discours de la méthode

## karma: action, and the residue action leaves — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/karma

Glossary

# karma कर्मन्

action, and the residue action leaves

Sanskrit · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / karma

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Action](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/action) · [Responsibility](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/responsibility) · [Fate](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/fate) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Morality](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/morality) · [Life](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/life)

## What the term does

Karma names action and, by extension, the mechanism by which action shapes what comes next: a deed leaves a disposition, and the disposition tends to reproduce itself. In the Upaniṣadic and Buddhist traditions this is the reason for continuity between lives, but the concept is already doing work within a single life, where it is offered as an account of why the same person behaves consistently. The Gītā's response to the burden of karma is not to escape action but to act without attachment to its fruit, which is a claim about how action can stop accumulating.

## The reading the sources do not support

Used in English as a synonym for fate or for retribution, as though something external is keeping accounts. The Indian concept is a claim about the causal consequences of one's own activity, and the Gītā in particular is arguing that the causal chain can be interrupted.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Philosophy of law](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-law) · [Philosophy of education](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-education)

## katharsis: purgation, cleansing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/katharsis

Glossary

# katharsis κάθαρσις

purgation, cleansing

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / katharsis

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Beauty](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/beauty) · [Experience](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/experience) · [Spirit](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/spirit) · [Judgment](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/judgment)

## What the term does

Aristotle uses the word once, in the definition of tragedy in the Poetics, and says that tragedy effects through pity and fear the katharsis of those feelings. Because he never explains it there, the passage has carried an outsized commentary: readings range from medical purgation of the emotions to their intellectual clarification through the structure of the plot. The Poetics also uses the term elsewhere for ritual purification, which is part of why the medical reading gained ground.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as 'emotional release' or as catharsis in the modern therapeutic sense. Aristotle is describing something the form of a tragedy accomplishes on an audience, not something a person does to feel better.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## li (principle 理) and li (ritual 禮): two entirely distinct concepts that English renders identically — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/li

Glossary

# li (principle 理) and li (ritual 禮) 理 / 禮

two entirely distinct concepts that English renders identically

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / li (principle 理) and li (ritual 禮)

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Order](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/order) · [Method](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/method) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Virtue](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/virtue)

## What the term does

A collision in transliteration that causes real confusion. 理 (li) is 'pattern' or 'principle' — the structure that makes a thing the kind of thing it is, central to Zhu Xi, where investigating things means coming to grasp their li. 禮 (li) is 'ritual propriety' — the body of ceremonial and social forms that Confucius treats as the medium through which ren is realised. The two appear side by side in the same texts and are joined in the Neo-Confucian claim that ritual is the expression of principle, but they are not the same term, and a reader meeting 'li' in a translation has no way to tell which one is meant without the character.

## The reading the sources do not support

The homophone is not merely a hazard for readers — it is a named source of real interpretive error, because the Neo-Confucian doctrine that human nature is li in one sense and that its expression is li in the other is precisely about holding the two together. Reduced to one English word, the argument becomes vacuous.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Baruch Spinoza](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/baruch-spinoza) (1) , [Ludwig Wittgenstein](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ludwig-wittgenstein) (1) , [Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (1) , [Mazu Daoyi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/mazu-daoyi) (1) , [Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz) (2) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1) , [Wang Yangming](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/wang-yangming) (1)

## logos: account, reason, speech, proportion — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/logos

Glossary

# logos λόγος

account, reason, speech, proportion

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / logos

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Reason](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/reason) · [Language](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/language) · [Truth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/truth) · [Order](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/order) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding)

## What the term does

Logos carries a family of senses that English splits across several words: the reasoned account one gives of something, the faculty that produces it, the speech in which it is delivered, and — in Heraclitus and the Stoics — the rational order of the world itself. Heraclitus's logos is the principle by which things are what they are, and it is famously the thing people fail to understand even when they hear it. The Stoics took it as the active rational principle pervading matter. John's Gospel opens by identifying Christ with it, which is the route by which the term entered theology.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'word' alone, as in the Gospel prologue, or as 'logic' alone. Neither covers the political and rhetorical sense in which giving a logos of something means being able to defend it — the sense Socrates asks for and never quite receives.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic)

## māyā: power of appearance; the tendency of the world to seem self-standing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/maya

Glossary

# māyā माया

power of appearance; the tendency of the world to seem self-standing

Sanskrit · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / māyā

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Existence](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/existence) · [Truth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/truth) · [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Experience](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/experience) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding)

## What the term does

In Advaita Vedānta, māyā is the principle by which the single reality appears as many things, and by which that appearance is taken for what is real. It is neither a delusion a person inflicts on themselves nor a second reality standing over against brahman; it is described as beginningless and as neither real nor unreal, which is a technical placement rather than a hedge. Śaṅkara's point is that the plurality we report is not false in the way a mirage is false — it is not nothing — but it is not independent, and the whole work of the teaching is to see through that independence.

## The reading the sources do not support

Rendered as 'illusion' and taken to mean that the world does not exist. Advaita's claim is that the world is not what it seems to be — it lacks independent reality — rather than that there is nothing there. The two readings lead to entirely different ethics, and the second is the one the school rejects.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Michel de Montaigne](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/michel-de-montaigne) (1) , [Baruch Spinoza](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/baruch-spinoza) (1) , [Socrates](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/socrates) (1) , [G. W. F. Hegel](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/g-w-f-hegel) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (1) , [Nishitani Keiji](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/nishitani-keiji) (1) , [Francis Bacon](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/francis-bacon) (1) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1)

## ming: mandate, decree, what is allotted — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/ming

Glossary

# ming 命

mandate, decree, what is allotted

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / ming

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Fate](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/fate) · [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god) · [Life](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/life) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Responsibility](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/responsibility) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding)

## What the term does

Ming is the term for what is assigned to one and cannot be altered: the Zhongyong opens by saying that what Heaven mandates is called nature. It carries both the sense of a command and the sense of a portion one receives, and the two readings coexist — in the Analects, knowing ming is part of what makes a person able to act without anxiety, because it marks the line beyond which effort is useless. Fatalism in the sense of passive resignation is generally not what the texts recommend; the point is to know where action is effective and where it is not, so as not to waste the first on the second.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'fate' and read as determinism. The Mencian notion is closer to a limit condition: ming is what you cannot do anything about, and the ethical task is to locate that boundary accurately, not to submit to it in general.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of science](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-science)

## mu: the syllable of the first koan; no / nothing / without — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/mu

Glossary

# mu 無

the syllable of the first koan; no / nothing / without

Japanese / Chinese · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / mu

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Awakening](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/awakening) · [Limits](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/limits) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Inquiry](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/inquiry) · [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind)

## What the term does

The single-syllable reply Zhaozhou gave when asked whether a dog has Buddha-nature, and the subject of the first case of the Gateless Barrier. The tradition normally leaves it untranslated, and this is deliberate: the received doctrine answers the question yes, so the reply cannot be doing the work of a proposition. Wumen's instruction is to hold the syllable itself — to bring it before oneself continuously and not to let it become a puzzle one tries to solve by analysis. It is described as a red-hot iron ball one cannot swallow or spit out, which is a description of a method rather than of a doctrine.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as the Buddhist doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā), and therefore as an answer to the question. Japanese Zen commentary is explicit that taking it as a denial is the classic error, and that the syllable is not the same term as the emptiness of the sutras even though the character is the same.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## niṣkāma karma: action without craving for its fruit — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/niskama-karma

Glossary

# niṣkāma karma निष्काम कर्म

action without craving for its fruit

Sanskrit · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / niṣkāma karma

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Action](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/action) · [Desire](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/desire) · [Freedom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/freedom) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Equanimity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/equanimity) · [Responsibility](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/responsibility)

## What the term does

The Gītā's practical doctrine: act, and act fully, but do not let the action be motivated by its result. The point is not that results do not matter but that the agent's relation to them is what determines whether the action binds. Since the results are not within one's control, tying one's satisfaction to them guarantees disturbance whether or not they arrive. This is why the Gītā can present the same act as liberating for one person and binding for another, and why it is a teaching about agency rather than about the content of the act.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as indifference to outcomes, and so as an alibi for carelessness. The Gītā requires the act to be performed properly and completely; what is given up is the claim on the result, not the effort in the doing.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy) · [Philosophy of law](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-law) · [Philosophy of education](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-education)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Hannah Arendt](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/hannah-arendt) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (3) , [Mazu Daoyi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/mazu-daoyi) (1) , [Augustine of Hippo](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/augustine-of-hippo) (1) , [Voltaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/voltaire) (1) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (1)

## nous: intellect; direct apprehension — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/nous

Glossary

# nous νοῦς

intellect; direct apprehension

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / nous

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind) · [Reason](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/reason) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Thinking](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/thinking)

## What the term does

Nous is the faculty by which first principles are grasped, as distinct from the discursive reasoning that works out their consequences. Aristotle says the principles of demonstration cannot themselves be demonstrated, so something must apprehend them immediately, and that is nous. Anaxagoras had made Nous the cosmic ordering principle, and Aristotle's unmoved mover is described as nous that thinks itself — the thought thinking thought, which is both the peak of his metaphysics and one of the most argued-about passages in the corpus.

## The reading the sources do not support

Treated as intuition in the modern psychological sense of a hunch. Nous is a cognitive achievement on the basis of training, not a feeling about what is probably true.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## oikeiōsis: appropriation; coming to recognise something as one's own — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/oikeiosis

Glossary

# oikeiōsis οἰκείωσις

appropriation; coming to recognise something as one's own

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / oikeiōsis

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Humanity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/humanity) · [Love](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/love) · [Community](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/community) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/ethics) · [Justice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/justice) · [Otherness](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/otherness) · [Relation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/relation)

## What the term does

The Stoic account of how moral concern extends. A creature begins by being attached to itself and its own constitution, then to its offspring, then to those who share its household and city, and finally — in the fully developed rational being — to all human beings as such, because they share in reason. Hierocles's image is of concentric circles drawn around a centre which one then works to contract. The doctrine is the Stoic answer to why a rational agent should care about strangers, and it is one of the ancestor ideas of later cosmopolitanism and of modern moral-circles arguments.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy) · [Philosophy of law](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-law)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (1) , [Martin Buber](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/martin-buber) (2) , [Augustine of Hippo](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/augustine-of-hippo) (2) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (2) , [Diogenes of Sinope](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/diogenes-of-sinope) (1)

## ordo amoris: the order of loves — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/ordo-amoris

Glossary

# ordo amoris

the order of loves

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / ordo amoris

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Love](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/love) · [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god) · [Desire](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/desire) · [Good](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/good) · [Morality](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/morality) · [Order](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/order) · [Will](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/will)

## What the term does

Augustine's account of virtue as rightly ordered love: a good will is one that loves things in proportion to their worth, God first, then creatures in their proper measure, and none of them as though it were the highest good. The concept is Augustinian rather than directly scriptural, and it was developed before him in Ambrose and in the Neoplatonic hierarchy of goods. It underlies the later Christian analysis of sin as disordered love rather than as the pursuit of evil, and it is why Augustine treats the Fall as a matter of what is loved rather than of what is known.

## The reading the sources do not support

Reduced to 'love the right things', which loses the proportional structure. What makes the doctrine do work is that a love can be too great as well as misplaced, and the sin can lie in the degree rather than the object.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Philosophy of religion](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-religion)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Baruch Spinoza](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/baruch-spinoza) (1) , [Socrates](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/socrates) (1) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1) , [Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (1) , [Augustine of Hippo](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/augustine-of-hippo) (1) , [Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz) (1) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (1)

## phronēsis: practical wisdom; sound judgement about what to do — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/phronesis

Glossary

# phronēsis φρόνησις

practical wisdom; sound judgement about what to do

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / phronēsis

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Wisdom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/wisdom) · [Judgment](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/judgment) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/ethics) · [Action](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/action) · [Morality](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/morality) · [Reason](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/reason)

## What the term does

Phronēsis is the intellectual virtue that governs action: the capacity to see what a situation calls for and to deliberate well about it. Aristotle distinguishes it sharply from scientific knowledge, because its subject matter is particular and changeable and cannot be demonstrated; it is also distinguished from craft, because its end is acting well rather than producing a product. It cannot be forgotten the way a fact can, and Aristotle holds that it is inseparable from the moral virtues — one cannot be practically wise without being good, and cannot be good without judgement.

## The reading the sources do not support

Treated as cleverness or as general intelligence. Aristotle separates it from deinotēs, mere cleverness, on the ground that cleverness is equally available to someone aiming at the wrong end. Phronēsis includes knowing what the end is.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## prohairesis: the faculty of choice; what is up to us — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/prohairesis

Glossary

# prohairesis προαίρεσις

the faculty of choice; what is up to us

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / prohairesis

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Choice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/choice) · [Freedom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/freedom) · [Responsibility](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/responsibility) · [Autonomy](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/autonomy) · [Fate](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/fate) · [Will](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/will)

## What the term does

Prohairesis is Epictetus's central term: it names the power of choosing how to respond, and with it the whole of what he says is genuinely 'up to us'. Body, property, reputation, and office are not up to us; the use we make of impressions is. Every Stoic injunction to accept what happens depends on this partition, because what cannot be prevented can still be assented to or refused. Aristotle uses the same word for a decided choice that results from deliberation and is bound up with character, which is a narrower and different sense.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'free will', which makes it sound like a metaphysical claim about causation. Epictetus is making a practical partition between what one's own judgement covers and what it does not.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy) · [Philosophy of law](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-law)

## qi: the stuff and its dynamic configurations — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/qi

Glossary

# qi 氣

the stuff and its dynamic configurations

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / qi

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Life](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/life) · [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind) · [Cultivation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/cultivation) · [Change](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/change)

## What the term does

Qi is what things are made of, so far as early and later Chinese cosmology makes that claim, but the concept is inseparable from its motion and its condensation: qi gathers and disperses, and a thing is a temporary configuration of it rather than a substance that possesses it. The Mencian claim that one's qi can be cultivated, and the Neo-Confucian accounts of qi as the material aspect of the world against principle as its pattern, both depend on this. In medical and self-cultivation traditions it is the medium of vitality, which is where the word's popular English use comes from.

## The reading the sources do not support

Treated as an energy field or a force, in which case it becomes a physical quantity that can be measured. In the philosophical texts it is closer to matter that is never at rest, and the interesting questions are about how pattern and configuration relate to it.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind) · [Philosophy of science](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-science)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Baruch Spinoza](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/baruch-spinoza) (1) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (2) , [Xunzi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/xunzi) (1) , [Voltaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/voltaire) (1) , [George Berkeley](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/george-berkeley) (1) , [Friedrich Nietzsche](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/friedrich-nietzsche) (1) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (1)

## ren: humaneness; being fully responsive to others as persons — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/ren

Glossary

# ren 仁

humaneness; being fully responsive to others as persons

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / ren

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Benevolence](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/benevolence) · [Humanity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/humanity) · [Virtue](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/virtue) · [Love](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/love) · [Relation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/relation) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/ethics) · [Community](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/community)

## What the term does

Ren is the central virtue of the Analects. The graph is composed of the element for 'person' with the element for 'two', and although that etymology is not decisive it is the traditional sense of the word: ren is what holds between persons, articulated by Confucius as loving others and by later commentators as the fully developed capacity to respond to others as persons. Confucius refuses to define it. Asked repeatedly, he answers with different things on each occasion, and his interlocutors' own conduct is usually what changes the answer — which is characteristic of how the text teaches.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'benevolence', which is close but tends to become a disposition of kindness. Ren in the Analects is tested by ritual performance and political conduct, and it is easier to say what someone with ren would do in a circumstance than what ren is.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (2) , [Martin Buber](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/martin-buber) (2) , [Augustine of Hippo](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/augustine-of-hippo) (2) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (2)

## res cogitans / res extensa: thinking substance and extended substance — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/res-cogitans-res-extensa

Glossary

# res cogitans / res extensa

thinking substance and extended substance

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / res cogitans / res extensa

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind) · [Existence](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/existence) · [Certainty](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/certainty) · [Soul](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/soul) · [Science](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/science) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being)

## What the term does

The two kinds of substance Descartes argues for in the Meditations: mind, whose whole nature is to think, and body, whose whole nature is to occupy space. Each is intelligible without the other, which is how the real distinction is argued, and it leaves the problem that has occupied philosophy since — how two substances with nothing in common interact. Descartes's answer, that the union of mind and body is known through the ordinary course of life rather than through philosophy, was widely treated as evasive, and the version of it that became notorious was the occasionalism of his followers.

## The reading the sources do not support

Called 'Cartesian dualism' as though it were a single doctrine, and then treated as obviously false. The interesting question is not whether the two substances are separate but why the argument for their separability was so persuasive to a whole century.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[René Descartes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/rene-descartes) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (1) , [Nishitani Keiji](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/nishitani-keiji) (1) , [Voltaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/voltaire) (1) , [George Berkeley](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/george-berkeley) (1) , [Plotinus](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/plotinus) (1) , [Charles Sanders Peirce](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/charles-sanders-peirce) (1) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (1)

## satori: awakening; the direct seeing a practitioner works toward — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/satori

Glossary

# satori 悟り

awakening; the direct seeing a practitioner works toward

Japanese · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / satori

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Awakening](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/awakening) · [Enlightenment](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/enlightenment) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind)

## What the term does

Satori is the Zen term for the experience of seeing one's own nature, and the tradition is careful that it is not a matter of acquiring information: the distinction between gradual cultivation and sudden awakening is a disagreement internal to Chan and Zen rather than between Zen and its rivals. The tradition also insists that awakening is not the end of practice — the Song and Japanese masters both return to the point that without continued practice an awakening is a place to sit rather than a thing that changes a life.

## The reading the sources do not support

Presented as enlightenment in the sense of a permanent achieved state, or as a peak experience. The Chan sources repeatedly warn that treating the experience as a possession reinstates exactly the grasping it was supposed to end.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind) · [Philosophy of education](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-education)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## sub specie aeternitatis: under the aspect of eternity — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/sub-specie-aeternitatis

Glossary

# sub specie aeternitatis

under the aspect of eternity

Latin · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / sub specie aeternitatis

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Eternity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/eternity) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Freedom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/freedom) · [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god) · [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge) · [Time](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/time)

## What the term does

Spinoza's phrase for the standpoint from which things are understood as following necessarily from the nature of God or substance, rather than as contingent events in a particular duration. In the Ethics it is tied to the third kind of knowledge, scientia intuitiva, and it grounds his claim that the mind's blessedness is not a reward for virtue but is virtue itself. In the Ethics the same standpoint requires that one see things in their necessity, which is why Spinoza holds that adequate knowledge of things removes the passions that depend on treating them as contingent.

## The reading the sources do not support

Used loosely to mean 'objectively' or 'in the long run'. Spinoza means a determinate cognitive achievement: seeing a thing's place in the necessary order of nature.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Michel de Montaigne](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/michel-de-montaigne) (1) , [Baruch Spinoza](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/baruch-spinoza) (1) , [Socrates](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/socrates) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (2) , [Augustine of Hippo](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/augustine-of-hippo) (1) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (1) , [Francis Bacon](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/francis-bacon) (1)

## śūnyatā: emptiness; absence of own-being — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/sunyata

Glossary

# śūnyatā शून्यता

emptiness; absence of own-being

Sanskrit · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / śūnyatā

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Existence](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/existence) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Truth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/truth) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind) · [Limits](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/limits)

## What the term does

In the Prajñāpāramitā literature and in Nāgārjuna's Madhyamaka, śūnyatā is the claim that things lack svabhāva — own-being, the intrinsic nature in virtue of which a thing would be what it is independently of anything else. It is an analysis of dependence rather than a claim that nothing exists: precisely because things are empty of own-being, they arise and cease in dependence on conditions. Nāgārjuna's argument in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā is that this applies to concepts as well as to things, so that emptiness is not itself a thing one can cling to.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as 'nothingness' or as a form of nihilism. The Prajñāpāramitā texts themselves warn against this reading, and the Diamond Sutra's constant qualification — what is called a dharma is not a dharma — is designed partly to prevent emptiness from hardening into a position.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[G. W. F. Hegel](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/g-w-f-hegel) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (1) , [Nishitani Keiji](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/nishitani-keiji) (1) , [Voltaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/voltaire) (1) , [George Berkeley](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/george-berkeley) (1) , [Giambattista Vico](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/giambattista-vico) (1) , [Ralph Waldo Emerson](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ralph-waldo-emerson) (1) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (1)

## tawḥīd: affirming oneness; the unity of God — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/tawhid

Glossary

# tawḥīd توحيد

affirming oneness; the unity of God

Arabic · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / tawḥīd

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Faith](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/faith) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Truth](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/truth) · [Eternity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/eternity)

## What the term does

Tawḥīd is the affirmation that God is one, without partner, and the term names both the doctrine and the act of affirming it. In falsafa and kalām it becomes a much stronger claim than mere numerical monotheism: al-Ghazālī, Ibn Rushd, and the Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite theologians fought over whether God's attributes are identical with his essence, since distinct real attributes would compromise the unity being affirmed. The debate generated a great deal of Islamic philosophy of language, because the question of what it means to predicate something of God turns on how reference to a unique being works.

## The reading the sources do not support

Treated as simply 'monotheism', which loses the technical dispute it names. The philosophical content is in the question of what is being denied when plurality is denied of God, and it is that question, not the counting of gods, that the theologians were arguing about.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of language](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-language)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Baruch Spinoza](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/baruch-spinoza) (1) , [G. W. F. Hegel](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/g-w-f-hegel) (1) , [Anselm of Canterbury](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/anselm-of-canterbury) (1) , [Nishitani Keiji](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/nishitani-keiji) (1) , [Voltaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/voltaire) (1) , [George Berkeley](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/george-berkeley) (1) , [Giambattista Vico](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/giambattista-vico) (1) , [Ralph Waldo Emerson](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ralph-waldo-emerson) (1)

## telos: end, completion, the point of a thing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/telos

Glossary

# telos τέλος

end, completion, the point of a thing

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / telos

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Meaning](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/meaning) · [Action](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/action) · [Good](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/good) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Order](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/order) · [Life](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/life)

## What the term does

The telos of something is what its activity is directed toward, in the sense of what completes it rather than what merely stops it. Aristotle's natural philosophy is teleological throughout: an acorn's telos is the oak, not because the acorn aims at it consciously but because that is the form its development realises. Ethics inherits the same structure — eudaimonia is the telos of human life, and the virtues are organised around it. Modern science abandoned natural teleology, which is why Aristotle's biology reads so oddly to a contemporary reader, and why the reintroduction of teleological language into biology remains contested.

## The reading the sources do not support

Read as conscious purpose or intention. Aristotelian teleology does not require a mind that intends the end; it requires only a form that governs development. The confusion of these two is what makes 'argument from design' look like it follows from Aristotle when it does not.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Philosophy of language](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-language)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Baruch Spinoza](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/baruch-spinoza) (1) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1) , [Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (1) , [Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz) (1) , [Nishitani Keiji](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/nishitani-keiji) (1) , [Voltaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/voltaire) (2) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (1)

## teshuvah: return; repentance — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/teshuvah

Glossary

# teshuvah תְּשׁוּבָה

return; repentance

Hebrew · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / teshuvah

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Responsibility](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/responsibility) · [Morality](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/morality) · [Self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) · [Freedom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/freedom) · [Character](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/character) · [God](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/god)

## What the term does

Teshuvah means turning back or returning, and it names both the act of repentance and the state of being restored. Maimonides devotes a section of the Mishneh Torah to its laws and specifies its conditions in some detail: the wrong must be acknowledged, the harm repaired where repair is possible, and the same situation resisted when it recurs — so that the test of teshuvah is behavioural rather than emotional. The return to oneself is part of the word's structure, which is why the tradition reads it as a return to one's own nature rather than only as an approach to God.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'repentance' and understood as regret. The Maimonidean conditions make the concept a matter of changed conduct under a repeated test, not of a feeling about a past act.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy)

## tikkun olam: repairing the world — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/tikkun-olam

Glossary

# tikkun olam תִּקּוּן עוֹלָם

repairing the world

Hebrew · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / tikkun olam

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Action](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/action) · [Responsibility](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/responsibility) · [Justice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/justice) · [Community](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/community) · [Hope](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/hope)

## What the term does

The phrase occurs in the Mishnah and in the prayer book with a narrower legal sense — enactments made 'for the good order of the world' — and was given a cosmological reading in Lurianic kabbalah, where it names the human task of gathering the sparks dispersed in the breaking of the vessels. The modern social-justice sense, in which it means working for a better society, is a twentieth-century extension of the phrase rather than its earlier legal meaning. The three senses are often conflated in popular use, which makes the term's history invisible.

## The reading the sources do not support

Assumed to be an ancient term for social activism. The legal sense is older, the kabbalistic sense is medieval, and the political sense is modern; a claim about what 'the tradition' always meant by tikkun olam usually reflects one of the three rather than all.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy) · [Philosophy of law](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-law)

## ubuntu: the quality of being a person; humaneness — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/ubuntu

Glossary

# ubuntu

the quality of being a person; humaneness

Nguni Bantu · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / ubuntu

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Humanity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/humanity) · [Community](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/community) · [Self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) · [Relation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/relation) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/ethics) · [Otherness](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/otherness)

## What the term does

Ubuntu is built on the stem -ntu with the class prefix for persons, and the maxim usually given for it is umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu — a person is a person through other persons. It states a relation between personhood and community that is metaphysical as well as ethical: being a person is not given at birth but realised through participation in relations with others. Contemporary African philosophy holds it variously as a moral theory, as a critique of liberal individualism, and as a claim about the structure of agency, and the disagreements between those readings are active rather than settled.

## The reading the sources do not support

Reduced to 'I am because we are' as a slogan, and then treated as a straightforward communitarianism. The stronger claim in the literature is that personhood is graduated and can be lost — which is not a thesis any individualist premise would generate, nor a simple preference for the group.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/ethics) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Chandogya Upanisad](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/chandogya-upanisad) (1) , [Heraclitus](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/heraclitus) (1) , [Ovid](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ovid) (1) , [René Descartes](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/rene-descartes) (1) , [Yunmen Wenyan](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/yunmen-wenyan) (1) , [Aristotle](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/aristotle) (1) , [Mazu Daoyi](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/mazu-daoyi) (1) , [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/jean-paul-sartre) (1)

## vital force (force vitale): a putatively African concept of being as life-force — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/vital-force

Glossary

# vital force (force vitale)

a putatively African concept of being as life-force

French (as used in African philosophy) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / vital force (force vitale)

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Humanity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/humanity) · [Understanding](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/understanding) · [Critique](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/critique) · [Method](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/method)

## What the term does

Prospero Tempels's Bantu Philosophy (1945) argued that the ontology underlying the Bantu languages treats being as force rather than as substance, with God as the source of a vitality that all things possess in different degrees. The thesis was taken up by Placide Franssen and others and, more importantly, rejected. Paulin Hountondji, Fabien Eboussi-Boulaga, and Marcien Towa argued that Tempels constructed a system no African thinker had held, that the resulting 'ethnophilosophy' took anonymous collective representations as philosophy, and that its effect was to deny Africans the possibility of individual critical thought. The concept is therefore best read as a claim about how African philosophy was constructed by its outside interpreters.

## The reading the sources do not support

Presented as an African doctrine that scholars later criticised. It is more nearly the reverse: the critique is what the philosophical literature considers the substantive contribution, and 'vital force' survives mainly as the position that defined the debate.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Logic](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/logic)

## Thinkers who work with this term

[Baruch Spinoza](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/baruch-spinoza) (1) , [Ludwig Wittgenstein](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ludwig-wittgenstein) (1) , [Seneca](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/seneca) (1) , [Voltaire](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/voltaire) (1) , [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) (1) , [George Berkeley](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/george-berkeley) (1) , [Diogenes of Sinope](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/diogenes-of-sinope) (1) , [Alfred North Whitehead](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/alfred-north-whitehead) (1)

## wu wei: non-coercive action; acting without forcing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/wu-wei

Glossary

# wu wei 無為

non-coercive action; acting without forcing

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / wu wei

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Action](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/action) · [Way](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/way) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Power](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/power) · [Simplicity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/simplicity) · [Freedom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/freedom)

## What the term does

Wu wei does not mean inactivity. It means acting so that the action does not depend on effortful assertion — the sage's effectiveness comes from the alignment of what he does with the way things actually move, so that nothing is done 'artificially' in the sense of being imposed against the grain. The result is described in terms of not contending, and the political application is that a ruler who governs this way does not need to compel. The concept is also used by the Legalists, where it describes the ruler delegating to a functioning system — a very different practical content for the same phrase.

## The reading the sources do not support

Translated as 'doing nothing' or as 'effortless action', and then read as a recommendation of passivity. The Daodejing is full of claims about how effective wu wei is, which would be incoherent if no action were involved.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy) · [Philosophy of science](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-science)

## Thinkers who work with this term

## xin and xing: the heart-mind, and the nature one is born with — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/xin-and-xing

Glossary

# xin and xing 心 / 性

the heart-mind, and the nature one is born with

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / xin and xing

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/mind) · [Human Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/human-nature) · [Self](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/self) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Cultivation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/cultivation) · [Knowledge](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/knowledge)

## What the term does

Xin is conventionally translated 'heart-mind' because it covers both thought and feeling: the seat of intention, emotion, and cognition at once, and the thing a person has to rectify. Xing is a thing's nature — what it is by birth, and in Mencius what Heaven has mandated. The relation between them is the central argument of later Confucian thought: Mencius holds that xing is good and that the work consists in recovering and extending it; Xunzi holds that xing is bad in the sense of being raw and unformed; and in Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming the question becomes whether xin is identical with xing or distinct, which is a difference that determines whether moral cultivation is a matter of investigating things or of rectifying intentions.

## The reading the sources do not support

'Mind' alone for xin loses the affective half, and then Mencian arguments look like claims about cognition. English also lacks the split between nature-as-what-one-is and nature-as-the-world that the Chinese does not make here.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Epistemology](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/epistemology) · [Philosophy of mind](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-mind)

## zhongyong: equilibrium and constancy; not the mean between extremes — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/zhongyong

Glossary

# zhongyong 中庸

equilibrium and constancy; not the mean between extremes

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / zhongyong

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Moderation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/moderation) · [Order](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/order) · [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Practice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/practice) · [Cultivation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/cultivation) · [Equanimity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/equanimity)

## What the term does

Zhong names the state before joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have been aroused — an equilibrium that is not itself a feeling — while yong names constancy or the steady application of the way. Once the feelings are aroused and each reaches its due measure, the state is called harmony, and it is the cultivated condition the text is after. Zhu Xi makes zhong the correct measure of the mind before arousal and he the appropriate expression once aroused; together they are described as the great root and the universal path.

## The reading the sources do not support

'The golden mean' and 'moderation' are the established English renderings and both import the idea of splitting a difference between two extremes. The Chinese term is not about the size of a response but about its measure relative to the situation, and it is combined with yong, which is a claim about constancy rather than about avoiding excess.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Philosophy of science](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-science) · [Philosophy of education](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-education)

## ziran: self-so; what is so of itself — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary/ziran

Glossary

# ziran 自然

self-so; what is so of itself

Chinese (pinyin) · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / ziran

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Nature](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/nature) · [Way](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/way) · [Simplicity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/simplicity) · [Freedom](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/freedom) · [Order](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/order) · [Being](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/being)

## What the term does

Ziran literally means 'so-of-itself' and was originally an adverbial pair, describing the way something is without an external cause rather than naming a domain of things. The Daodejing's statement that humans follow earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows dao, and dao follows ziran is the pivot: it makes ziran the last term, which is why translating it as 'nature' with a definite article changes the argument. The modern Chinese and Japanese word for nature is this phrase, in a sense that arrived later.

## The reading the sources do not support

Rendered as 'nature', which invites the reading that dao follows the natural world. The pre-modern sense is that dao follows no prescription at all — it is the condition of being so of itself. This is one of the terms where the modern meaning of the graph rather than its original sense is what most translations use.

## Where it sits in the discipline

[Metaphysics](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/metaphysics) · [Political philosophy](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/political-philosophy) · [Philosophy of science](https://www.philosophydef.com/branches/philosophy-of-science)

## History of Philosophy: From Ancient Greece to Today | Philosophy Defined

Source: https://www.philosophydef.com/history-of-philosophy

The long view

# History of Philosophy: From Ancient Greece to Today

The history of philosophy is a history of arguments that never quite closed: each period inherits its questions from the last, answers them differently, and passes what remains open forward.

Philosophy Defined · Last reviewed 2026-10-01 · [How guides are written](https://www.philosophydef.com/editorial-policy)

On this page

1.  [Ancient philosophy: the questions are named](#section-1)
2.  [Medieval philosophy: reason meets revelation](#section-2)
3.  [Early modern philosophy: the turn to the knower](#section-3)
4.  [Modern philosophy: systems and their collapse](#section-4)
5.  [Contemporary philosophy: the professional and the global](#section-5)
6.  [How to read the history](#section-6)
7.  [FAQ](#faq)
8.  [Further reading](#further-reading)

## Short answer

Philosophy's history runs from the sixth-century BCE inquirers of Miletus, through the classical systems of Plato and Aristotle and the medieval work of Augustine, Ibn Sina, Maimonides, and Aquinas, to Descartes and the early moderns, Kant and German Idealism, and the analytic, phenomenological, and global debates of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Read it as a chain of open questions rather than a gallery of opinions.

## Ancient philosophy: the questions are named

The Western story opens around Miletus in the sixth century BCE, when thinkers first proposed natural rather than mythical explanations of the cosmos. Heraclitus made change the central fact; Parmenides denied it; their quarrel seeded metaphysics. In Athens, Socrates (469–399 BCE) turned philosophy toward ethics — how to live — and made argument itself the method, accepting death rather than abandoning the examined life.

Plato founded the Academy and wrote dialogues whose questions are still assigned to students: what justice is, what knowledge is, what the Forms would have to be. Aristotle organized the sciences, defined virtue as a mean between extremes, and gave logic its first system. The Hellenistic schools — Stoics, Epicureans, Skeptics — treated philosophy as the art of living well under uncertainty, which is why their passages still circulate as quotes.

The same centuries produced classical Chinese philosophy — Confucius, Mencius, Xunzi, Laozi, Zhuangzi — arguing over human nature, ritual, and the Way, and classical Indian philosophy, whose schools debated consciousness, causation, and liberation with a rigour the term “Eastern philosophy” hides rather than honours.

## Medieval philosophy: reason meets revelation

For roughly a thousand years the central problem was the relation between reason and revealed religion. Augustine fused Platonism with Christianity and wrote the Confessions, the first philosophical autobiography. In Baghdad and Córdoba, Al-Farabi, Avicenna (Ibn Sina), and Averroes (Ibn Rushd) transmitted and transformed Aristotle; al-Ghazali pressed the critique the philosophers had to answer; Maimonides did the same constructive work for Jewish thought.

The period ends with William of Ockham's razor and the late-medieval nominalists, who thinned the inherited metaphysics until the early moderns could rebuild. Quoting this era well requires care: the archive records which translation and which numbering a passage comes from, because medieval texts are cited differently in every tradition.

## Early modern philosophy: the turn to the knower

Descartes' Meditations (1641) made certainty the entry problem: doubt everything, keep only what survives. Spinoza and Leibniz built rationalist systems on that confidence; Locke, Berkeley, and Hume answered from the empiricist side, until Hume's scepticism about causation and the self woke Kant, as he said, from his dogmatic slumber.

The period also wrote the political philosophy the modern world still argues inside — Hobbes' Leviathan, Locke's toleration and property, Rousseau's general will — and Spinoza's and Hume's critiques of miracles, which redrew the border between philosophy and religion for good.

## Modern philosophy: systems and their collapse

Kant's critical philosophy (1781–1790) argued that experience is structured by the mind's own forms, that metaphysics exceeds possible knowledge, and that morality begins from autonomy. German Idealism — Fichte, Schelling, Hegel — tried to complete what Kant started; Hegel made history itself philosophical. Marx inverted Hegel; Kierkegaard and Nietzsche attacked the system from inside, and their attack is where existentialism begins.

Schopenhauer, Mill, and Darwin belong here too: the pessimist who took the will seriously, the utilitarian who argued liberty, and the naturalist who forced every account of mind and morality to face descent with modification. The archive's most-quoted Nietzsche and Mill passages all come from these decades.

## Contemporary philosophy: the professional and the global

The twentieth century split into vocabularies more than camps. The analytic tradition — Frege, Russell, Moore, Wittgenstein, then Quine and the postwar generations — made logic and language the instruments; phenomenology and existentialism — Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre, de Beauvoir, Merleau-Ponty — made lived experience the subject. Pragmatism (Peirce, James, Dewey) tested ideas by their consequences, and the Frankfurt School put philosophy back into political critique.

Since 1970 the discipline has professionalized and globalized: Rawls revived political philosophy, feminist and Africana philosophy restructured the canon's assumptions, philosophy of mind and language met cognitive science, and philosophy of AI — Turing's question reborn — became a working field. The debates are open, which is exactly why the archive quotes them with sources.

## How to read the history

Three habits make the history tractable. Read each thinker as answering a named predecessor, not as delivering timeless views. Date the works — a passage from 1650 is answering Descartes whether or not it names him. And keep the questions visible: what exists, what can be known, how to live, who decides. The periods are the changes those questions undergo.

The archive is organized to support this reading: every passage carries its work and locator, so a history can be checked against the texts rather than taken on authority.

## Frequently asked questions

### What are the main periods in the history of philosophy?

A common division: ancient (roughly 600 BCE–500 CE), medieval (500–1400), early modern (1400–1700), modern (1700–1900), and contemporary (1900–today). The dates are conventions; the questions are what carry across the boundaries.

### Who was the first philosopher?

In the Western tradition, Thales of Miletus (c. 600 BCE) is conventionally first, for proposing a natural explanation of the cosmos. Chinese and Indian philosophical traditions developed in the same centuries through figures such as Confucius, Laozi, and the Buddha, whose exact chronology is a matter of textual history rather than a single date.

### Why study the history of philosophy at all?

Because the failures are the most instructive parts: each classic position is a precisely worked-out answer to a question that is still open, and knowing how it failed tells you what any new answer must get past.

## Further reading

-   Anthony Kenny, A New History of Western Philosophy (2010)
-   Frederick Copleston, A History of Philosophy, vols. 1–9
-   Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entries by period and figure
