## The work in Marcus Aurelius’s thought

Marcus Aurelius (121–180 CE) was Roman emperor from 161 and a practicing Stoic who wrote private Greek notes later titled Meditations. He spent much of his reign on military campaigns along the Danube amid plague and political strain. [More on Marcus Aurelius](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/marcus-aurelius) .

Mencius (Meng Ke, c. 371–c. [More on Mencius](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/mencius) .

## The work in Ibn Khaldun’s thought

Ibn Khaldūn (1332–1406) served courts across the Maghrib and Egypt before composing the Muqaddimah as a prolegomenon to his universal history. ## The work in Arthur Schopenhauer’s thought

Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was a German philosopher of pessimism whose The World as Will and Representation fused Kantian phenomena with a blind metaphysical will. Largely ignored while Hegel dominated Berlin, he later won fame influencing artists and psychologists. [More on Arthur Schopenhauer](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/arthur-schopenhauer) .

## The work in Frantz Fanon’s thought

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Pensées are identified by fragment number — which numbering must be named. There is no single canonical numbering. The Brunschvicg (1897) and Lafuma (1951) systems differ, and a fragment number is meaningless without saying which it follows — a point the corpus flags where it records 'common numbering'. Pascal died before arranging the material, so the order of the fragments is editorial throughout.

## The work in Blaise Pascal’s thought

Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, and Christian apologist who invented an early calculator and advanced probability and fluid mechanics. After a decisive religious conversion, he defended Jansenism in the Provincial Letters and left unfinished Pensées. [More on Blaise Pascal](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/blaise-pascal) .

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Philosophical Investigations are identified by part and numbered remark (e.g. §116). Published after Wittgenstein's death from material he had reworked repeatedly. The first part is a numbered sequence of remarks; the second part is a later addition and its status is disputed. The archive cites § numbers, which is the standard reference.

## The work in Ludwig Wittgenstein’s thought

Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951), born in Vienna to a wealthy industrial family, studied engineering then logic with Russell at Cambridge. The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) aimed to draw limits to sense; he then left academic philosophy for years as a teacher and architect’s assistant. [More on Ludwig Wittgenstein](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ludwig-wittgenstein) .

1.  > What we do is to bring words back from their metaphysical to their everyday use.
    
    [Ludwig Wittgenstein: “What we do is to bring words back…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0086)
    
2.  > The meaning of a word is its use in the language.
    
    [Ludwig Wittgenstein: “The meaning of a word is its use…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0127)
    
3.  > Don’t think, but look!
    
    [Ludwig Wittgenstein: “Don’t think, but look!” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0423)
    
4.  > The most ordinary things escape notice precisely because they are ordinary.
    
    [Ludwig Wittgenstein: “The most ordinary things escape notice precisely because…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0488)

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Philosophy of Liberation are identified by section number (e.g. §1.1.2.2). Cited by section rather than page, and the sections are the ones in the English translation. Dussel reworked the book substantially between editions, so the edition is part of the citation.

## The work in Enrique Dussel’s thought

Enrique Dussel (1934–2023) was an Argentine-Mexican philosopher of liberation who wrote from geopolitical periphery—famously in Mexican exile—toward a worldwide philosophy. Philosophy of Liberation (1977) and later ethics of liberation fuse Levinasian exteriority with a critique of Eurocentric modernity since 1492. [More on Enrique Dussel](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/enrique-dussel) .

1.  > Before the ego cogito there is an ego conquiro; “I conquer” is the practical foundation of “I think.”
    
    [Enrique Dussel: “Before the ego cogito there is an ego…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0670)
    
2.  > From the “I conquer” applied to the Aztec and Inca world and all America, from the “I enslave” applied to Africans … from this “I” appears the Cartesian ego cogito.
    
    [Enrique Dussel: “From the “I conquer” applied to the Aztec…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0671)
    
3.  > Philosophy, when it is really philosophy and not sophistry or ideology, does not ponder philosophy. … Philosophy ponders the nonphilosophical; the reality.
    
    [Enrique Dussel: “Philosophy, when it is really philosophy and not…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0672)
    
4.  > Written from the periphery, for persons and peoples of the periphery, this book nonetheless also addresses readers in the center of the present world system.
    
    [Enrique Dussel: “Written from the periphery, for persons and peoples…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0673)

# Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch 六祖壇經

4 passages in this archive · Compiled c. 8th–13th century CE across successive recensions

[Works](https://www.philosophydef.com/works) / Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

Author

[Huineng](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/huineng)

Original title

六祖壇經 (Liùzǔ tánjīng)

Composed

Compiled c. 8th–13th century CE across successive recensions

English wording

From Philip Yampolsky (where the corpus records a translator)

Verification

Recorded from the corpus; individual pages state their level.

[What these levels mean](https://www.philosophydef.com/about#verification-levels)

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch are identified by chapter of the received edition (e.g. prajna chapter). The text exists in several substantially different recensions. The Dunhuang manuscript, the Huixin edition, the Zongbao edition of 1291, and the Ming text differ in length and in doctrine, and the Zongbao edition is much the longest. A chapter reference without naming the recension is therefore incomplete, and the corpus flags the Zongbao text on the entry that uses it.

## The work in Huineng’s thought

Huineng (638–713) is revered as the Sixth Patriarch of Chan (Zen) Buddhism in China; the Platform Sutra presents his autobiography and teachings. Historical layers of the text are complex; the legend contrasts an illiterate laborer with scholastic rivals. [More on Huineng](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/huineng) .

1.  > Bodhi originally has no tree; the bright mirror is not a stand. Fundamentally there is not a single thing — where could dust alight?
    
    [Huineng: “Bodhi originally has no tree; the bright mirror…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0207)
    
2.  > Who would have thought that self-nature is originally pure; who would have thought that self-nature is originally neither born nor destroyed.
    
    [Huineng: “Who would have thought that self-nature is originally…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0468)
    
3.  > It is not the wind that moves; it is not the flag that moves; it is your mind that moves.
    
    [Huineng: “It is not the wind that moves; it…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0678)
    
4.  > The Buddhist teaching is in the world; awakening is not apart from the world. To seek enlightenment apart from the world is like looking for a hare's horn.
    
    [Huineng: “The Buddhist teaching is in the world; awakening…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0679)

## The work in Simone de Beauvoir’s thought

Simone de Beauvoir (1908–1986) was a French existentialist philosopher and novelist whose The Second Sex (1949) transformed feminist theory. A Normalienne, she partnered intellectually with Sartre while building an independent oeuvre on ethics, aging, and politics. [More on Simone de Beauvoir](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/simone-de-beauvoir) .

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Record of Linji are identified by section of the record. A posthumous compilation by Linji's disciples, reworked across the Song. The corpus flags two entries as a translation and as abridged, which is the archive's way of saying that their wording does not come from the same edition as the rest.

## The work in Linji Yixuan’s thought

Linji Yixuan, who died in 866 CE, founded the Linji school — Rinzai in Japanese — one of the two Chan lineages that survived the Song reforms and the one that shaped Japanese Zen most deeply. He trained under Huangbo Xiyun after an initial period under Baizhang's disciple Chengshen, and his teaching community near modern Zhengding was known for its severity. [More on Linji Yixuan](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/linji-yixuan) .

1.  > Wherever you are, make yourself master; wherever you stand is real.
    
    [Linji Yixuan: “Wherever you are, make yourself master; wherever you…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0304)
    
2.  > If you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha; if you meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch; if you meet an arhat, kill the arhat.
    
    [Linji Yixuan: “If you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha;…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0680)
    
3.  > There is a true person of no rank who is always coming and going through the gates of your face.
    
    [Linji Yixuan: “There is a true person of no rank…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0681)
    
4.  > There is no place in Buddhism for special effort. Just be ordinary: put on your clothes, eat your food, and lie down when you are tired.
    
    [Linji Yixuan: “There is no place in Buddhism for special…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0682)

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Renjian Cihua are identified by numbered item (則). The corpus cites the work under its romanised title and under an English rendering on different pages. They are the same text, and the numbered item is what identifies a passage in it.

## The work in Wang Guowei’s thought

Wang Guowei (1877–1927) was a late Qing–Republican scholar who joined classical Chinese learning with Western aesthetics and philosophy. He wrote on tragedy, ci poetry, oracle bones, and the history of Song–Yuan drama. [More on Wang Guowei](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/wang-guowei) .

1.  > Those who in ancient or modern times achieved great enterprises and profound learning must pass through three realms: first, standing alone atop a high tower after the west wind withers the green trees, gazing to the end of the road at heaven's edge; second, the belt growing looser without regret, wasting away for the beloved; third, searching a thousand times in the crowd, then suddenly turning — and finding that person standing where the lanterns grow sparse.
    
    [Wang Guowei: “Those who in ancient or modern times achieved…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0174)
    
2.  > In the realm with a self, one views things through the self, so things take on one’s coloring. In the realm without a self, one views things through things, and no longer knows which is self and which is thing.
    
    [Wang Guowei: “In the realm with a self, one views…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0482)
    
3.  > Ci poetry takes jingjie — the aesthetic realm — as its highest: with jingjie it naturally attains a lofty style and famous lines of its own.
    
    [Wang Guowei: “Ci poetry takes jingjie — the aesthetic realm…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0688)
    
4.  > Jingjie is not a matter of scenery alone: joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness are also realms of the human heart. Whoever can write true scenery and true feeling may be said to have jingjie.
    
    [Wang Guowei: “Jingjie is not a matter of scenery alone:…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0689)

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Self-Reliance are identified by essay — no internal divisions. An essay rather than a book, and one of the most quoted in American letters. It has no numbered sections, so the archive cites the essay and quotes the sentence.

## The work in Ralph Waldo Emerson’s thought

Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was the American Transcendentalist essayist and lecturer who urged self-reliance and unbroken relation to nature and the Over-Soul. A former Unitarian minister in Concord, he gathered the Dial circle and mentored younger writers including Thoreau. [More on Ralph Waldo Emerson](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ralph-waldo-emerson) .

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Shūkyō to wa nanika (Religion and Nothingness) are identified by chapter, with page in the van bragt translation where recorded. The corpus records Van Bragt page numbers, which are the standard way to cite the English text; a page number without naming the translation is not usable, because the Japanese pagination is different.

## The work in Nishitani Keiji’s thought

Nishitani Keiji (1900–1990) was Nishida’s student and a central second-generation Kyoto School figure. Educated in Japan and briefly in Germany under Heidegger’s orbit, he taught at Kyoto University and wrote Religion and Nothingness (Japanese Shūkyō to wa nanika), which confronts modern nihilism through Zen and Mahāyāna emptiness. [More on Nishitani Keiji](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/nishitani-keiji) .

1.  > For what purpose do I exist?
    
    [Nishitani Keiji: “For what purpose do I exist?” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0652)
    
2.  > At the point of our deepest questioning of ourselves, the religious quest awakens in us.
    
    [Nishitani Keiji: “At the point of our deepest questioning of…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0653)
    
3.  > So long as the field of separation between within and without is not broken through, and so long as a conversion from that standpoint does not take place, the lack of unity and contradiction spoken of earlier cannot help but prevail among the things we take as real.
    
    [Nishitani Keiji: “So long as the field of separation between…” — source & context](https://www.philosophydef.com/quotes/q0654)
    
4.  > Nothingness in the sense of emptiness (śūnyatā) is not separate from being, but always in a relationship with being: being-sive-nothingness, nothingness-sive-being.

## How this work is cited

Passages inside The Analects are identified by book and chapter (e.g. lunyu 4.15). The Analects is a compiled record of sayings, not a work by Confucius. The common formula 'Confucius said' refers to a tradent whose words were assembled by later hands, and the book-and-chapter locator is what makes a passage findable in any edition.

## The work in Confucius’s thought

Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) taught in the late Spring and Autumn period amid the Zhou order’s political fragmentation. Born in the state of Lu, he briefly held local office and then spent years seeking rulers who would adopt ritual-based, virtue-centered government. [More on Confucius](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/confucius) .

## The work in Søren Kierkegaard’s thought

Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) was a Danish religious author and critic of Christendom who wrote under pseudonyms exploring aesthetic, ethical, and religious existence. Inheriting a melancholy family fortune, he attacked Hegelian system and lukewarm official faith in Copenhagen. [More on Søren Kierkegaard](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/soren-kierkegaard) .

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus are identified by decimal proposition number (e.g. 6.54). The proposition numbers are the citation and they are self-indexing: 6.54 is the seventh remark under 6.5. The corpus names the work both in full and as 'Tractatus'; the numbers are the same in both.

## The work in Ludwig Wittgenstein’s thought

Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951), born in Vienna to a wealthy industrial family, studied engineering then logic with Russell at Cambridge. The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) aimed to draw limits to sense; he then left academic philosophy for years as a teacher and architect’s assistant. [More on Ludwig Wittgenstein](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/ludwig-wittgenstein) .

Verification

Recorded from the corpus; individual pages state their level.

[What these levels mean](https://www.philosophydef.com/about#verification-levels)

## How this work is cited

Passages inside Zhuangzi are identified by chapter (篇) by name. Only the seven 'inner chapters' are generally accepted as Zhuangzi's own; the outer and miscellaneous chapters are the work of a school. Which layer a passage comes from is part of what the locator tells a reader.

## The work in Zhuangzi’s thought
